episode: The Polish-German War
headline: Germany invades Poland
photo: f:Bundesarchiv Bild 183-S55480, Polen, Explosion eines Sprengkommandos.jpg
article: At 4:45 on the morning of 1 September 1939 the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte, outside Danzig. Within hours roughly 1.5 million German troops crossed into Poland from the west, from East Prussia in the north and from Slovakia in the south. The Luftwaffe bombed airfields, railways and towns; the small town of Wieluń was flattened in one of the first raids of the war. Berlin justified the attack with a staged "Polish" raid on a German radio station at Gleiwitz the night before, carried out by SS men in Polish uniforms. Poland had mobilised late under Anglo-French pressure not to provoke Hitler and was strung out along an indefensible border. Britain and France issued ultimatums. Nobody in Warsaw expected them to arrive in time.

episode: World War Two Begins
headline: Britain and France declare war
photo: w:British and French declaration of war on Germany
article: On Sunday 3 September Britain's ultimatum to Germany expired at 11 a.m. and Neville Chamberlain told the country by radio that it was at war. France followed at 5 p.m. Australia, New Zealand and India were brought in at once; South Africa and Canada decided for themselves within days. Churchill came back into the government as First Lord of the Admiralty. That evening a U-boat sank the liner Athenia off Ireland, killing over a hundred passengers, and Britain assumed unrestricted submarine war had begun. In Poland, meanwhile, German armour broke through the frontier armies and pushed for Warsaw and Kraków. The declarations changed the scale of the conflict but not the fight on the ground. The French army made a token advance into the Saar and stopped. Poland was left to fight alone while its allies prepared.

episode: Poland on Her Own
headline: Poland fights alone
article: By the second week German spearheads were on the outskirts of Warsaw, and the capital prepared for siege under its mayor, Stefan Starzyński, who rallied the city on the radio. The Polish Poznań and Pomorze armies, bypassed in the west, turned and struck the German flank on the river Bzura on 9 September in the largest battle of the campaign. It briefly checked the advance before being encircled and ground down by armour and aircraft. Kraków had fallen on 6 September. The government left Warsaw for the south-east, hoping to hold a redoubt near the Romanian border until the Western allies attacked. At a meeting in Abbeville on 12 September, Britain and France agreed in effect not to. The Polish army was still fighting hard, but its strategy depended on help that was not coming.

episode: The Russians are Coming! - The Soviet Invasion of Poland
headline: The Soviet Union invades from the east
article: On 17 September the Red Army crossed Poland's eastern border with more than half a million men, claiming to protect Ukrainians and Belarusians after the "collapse" of the Polish state. It was the secret protocol of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact being carried out. Polish commanders ordered troops not to fight the Soviets except in self-defence; many fought anyway, and some were shot after surrendering. The Polish government and high command crossed into Romania that night and were interned. On 22 September German and Soviet officers held a joint handover and parade in Brest-Litovsk. Lwów surrendered to the Red Army the same day. Poland's hope of a south-eastern redoubt was gone. Two dictatorships were now dividing a country between them, and both intended to destroy its educated class.

episode: Poland is Crushed
headline: Warsaw surrenders
article: Warsaw endured a week of heavy artillery fire and air raids, culminating in "Black Monday", 25 September, when the Luftwaffe dropped hundreds of tonnes of bombs and incendiaries on a city without water or power. Thousands of civilians were killed. The garrison capitulated on 27 September and the Modlin fortress a day later. On 28 September Germany and the USSR signed a new treaty adjusting their border: Lithuania went into the Soviet sphere in exchange for more of central Poland for Germany. Polish units still held out on the Hel peninsula and in the east. In Paris, General Sikorski began forming a Polish government-in-exile and an army from those who escaped. Tens of thousands of Polish soldiers and airmen made their way west through Romania and Hungary to keep fighting.

episode: Poland Falls and China Rises
headline: The last Polish army lays down its arms
article: The last organised Polish formation, General Kleeberg's Independent Operational Group Polesie, fought its final battle near Kock and surrendered on 6 October. The campaign had lasted five weeks. Poland lost around 66,000 soldiers killed; Germany about 16,000. Hitler reviewed a victory parade in Warsaw on 5 October and the next day offered the West a "peace" based on the new facts. London and Paris rejected it. Western Poland was annexed outright to the Reich, the rest became the "General Government" under Hans Frank, and the east went to the USSR. Behind the front, SS Einsatzgruppen were already shooting Polish priests, teachers and Jews. In China, meanwhile, Chinese forces were holding a Japanese drive on Changsha, a reminder that a second war had been running in Asia since 1937.

episode: The Baltic in Stalin's Squeeze
headline: Stalin squeezes the Baltic states
article: With Poland divided, Moscow turned to the small states assigned to it. Estonia had signed a "mutual assistance" pact on 28 September under threat of invasion; Latvia signed on 5 October and Lithuania on 10 October, the last sweetened with the return of Vilnius, taken from Poland. Each treaty let the Red Army station tens of thousands of troops on its soil. Formal independence survived for now, but everyone understood what garrisons meant. Thousands of Baltic Germans were summoned "home to the Reich" under a separate deal with Berlin. Finland was invited to talks on the same terms and sent negotiators to Moscow on 12 October. On the Western Front, German and French troops faced each other in near silence, the beginning of what British newspapers came to call the Phoney War.

episode: The Submarine War
headline: A U-boat inside Scapa Flow
article: In the early hours of 14 October Kapitänleutnant Günther Prien took U-47 through a gap in the blockships guarding Scapa Flow, the Home Fleet's main anchorage in Orkney, and torpedoed the battleship Royal Oak. She capsized in minutes; 835 men and boys died. Prien slipped out the way he came and was received in Berlin as a hero. For the Royal Navy it was a humiliation that followed the loss of the carrier Courageous to a U-boat in September. The fleet was moved to temporary anchorages on Scotland's west coast while Scapa's defences were fixed. The war at sea, unlike the war on land, was already real: convoys had been reintroduced, merchant ships were being sunk weekly, and both sides were laying mines across the North Sea approaches.

episode: Stalin's Murderous Adventures - Occupation of Poland
headline: Terror in occupied Poland
article: Both occupiers set about dismantling Polish society. In the German-annexed west the "Intelligenzaktion" targeted teachers, priests, landowners and officials; tens of thousands were shot by the end of the year, often in forests near their towns. Jews were robbed, humiliated, forced from their homes and pushed toward the General Government, where Hans Frank took office in Kraków on 26 October. In the Soviet zone, staged "elections" on 22 October produced assemblies that asked to join the USSR, and the NKVD began arrests of officers, police and "class enemies" that would lead to mass deportations and, in spring 1940, the Katyn massacres. Nothing on this scale was hidden from the people living through it, though little reached the outside world in detail. The occupation of Poland was meant to be permanent, and it was planned as a racial and political project from the start.

episode: Molotov's Heel on Finland and the Phoney War
headline: Finland says no
article: The Finnish delegation led by Juho Paasikivi spent October and early November in Moscow. Stalin wanted the border on the Karelian Isthmus pushed back from Leningrad, several Gulf of Finland islands, and a naval base at Hanko, offering Soviet Karelian forest in return. Finland was willing to give some ground but not Hanko or its main defensive line. Talks broke down on 13 November. In the west, the Phoney War settled in: British Expeditionary Force divisions dug in along the Belgian border, French troops sat behind the Maginot Line, and RAF bombers dropped leaflets over Germany rather than bombs. The United States passed the "cash and carry" amendment to its Neutrality Acts on 4 November, letting Britain and France buy American arms if they paid and shipped them themselves.

episode: Hitler Almost Killed
headline: A bomb in the beer hall
article: On 8 November Hitler gave his annual speech in Munich's Bürgerbräukeller to mark the 1923 putsch. He cut it short to catch a train to Berlin and left thirteen minutes before a bomb hidden in a pillar behind the lectern exploded, killing eight people. It had been built and planted over many nights by Georg Elser, a carpenter acting alone. He was caught at the Swiss border the same evening. The regime blamed British intelligence, and the next day, in a separate operation, SS men kidnapped two British agents at Venlo on the Dutch border. Elser was held in concentration camps for most of the war and murdered at Dachau in April 1945. Hitler took the escape as proof of providence. Plans to attack France that autumn were postponed again, mainly because of weather.

episode: The Mysterious Threat to the Royal Navy - Magnetic Mines
headline: Magnetic mines close the Thames
article: German aircraft and U-boats had been laying a new weapon in British shipping lanes: a magnetic mine that sat on the seabed and fired when a steel hull passed overhead. Losses spiked in November, including the Dutch liner Simon Bolivar off Harwich with heavy loss of life, and the Thames estuary was at times almost closed. On the night of 22–23 November a mine dropped by parachute landed on mudflats at Shoeburyness. Two Royal Navy officers from HMS Vernon dismantled it by hand and worked out the mechanism. Within weeks the Admiralty had countermeasures: "degaussing" cables wrapped around hulls to neutralise their magnetism and minesweeping techniques that could set the mines off safely. It was an early example of the technical war that would run in parallel with the fighting.

episode: Will the Kriegsmarine Rule the Waves?
headline: The Rawalpindi goes down fighting
article: On 23 November the German battleships Scharnhorst and Gneisenau broke out into the North Atlantic between Iceland and the Faroes. They ran into HMS Rawalpindi, a P&O liner converted into an armed merchant cruiser with old six-inch guns. Her captain, Edward Kennedy, refused to surrender and fought until his ship was set ablaze and sank; 238 of her crew died. The German ships turned for home rather than risk the Home Fleet. The Kriegsmarine was small compared with the Royal Navy, but its surface raiders and U-boats forced Britain to spread its ships thin across the world's oceans. In the South Atlantic, the pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee had already sunk several merchant ships and was being hunted by a British cruiser force.

episode: The Winter War
headline: The Soviet Union attacks Finland
article: On 26 November Moscow claimed that Finnish artillery had shelled the Soviet border village of Mainila, killing Red Army soldiers. Finland denied it and the evidence points to a staged incident. The USSR renounced its non-aggression pact, and on 30 November the Red Army attacked along the whole border with roughly 450,000 men, while bombers struck Helsinki. A day later a puppet "Finnish Democratic Republic" under the exiled communist Otto Kuusinen was proclaimed at Terijoki and promptly recognised by Moscow. The Soviets expected a short campaign; some units were told not to cross into Sweden by mistake. Finland mobilised around 300,000 men under Marshal Mannerheim, short of artillery, anti-tank guns and aircraft, but fighting on home ground in deep forest and winter.

episode: The Invasion of Finland
headline: The Red Army stalls on the Mannerheim Line
article: The Red Army's main thrust on the Karelian Isthmus ran into the Mannerheim Line, a belt of trenches, concrete bunkers and tank obstacles far weaker than its later reputation but well sited. Soviet infantry attacked in dense waves across open ground with poor coordination between tanks, artillery and riflemen. Losses were heavy. The purges of 1937–38 had stripped the Red Army of experienced commanders, and political officers second-guessed tactical decisions. North of Lake Ladoga, Soviet columns pushed down narrow forest roads toward the Finnish "waist". The League of Nations expelled the USSR on 14 December, its last significant act. Abroad, Finland became a popular cause: volunteers and donations came from Sweden, Norway, Britain and the United States.

episode: Perkele! Finland Strikes Back
headline: The Finns cut the columns apart
article: Around Suomussalmi in the north and Tolvajärvi north of Ladoga, Finnish troops on skis cut long Soviet road columns into isolated pockets, which they called motti, after the word for a stacked cord of firewood. Each pocket was then starved, frozen and attacked piece by piece. At Tolvajärvi on 12 December the Finns won their first clear victory of the war. At Suomussalmi the Soviet 163rd Division was encircled, and the 44th Division sent to rescue it was destroyed on the Raate road in early January, leaving abandoned guns, tanks and horses along miles of forest. Temperatures fell below –30°C. Many Soviet soldiers lacked winter clothing and had never trained for forest fighting. The world press called it a miracle; Finnish commanders knew they could not keep it up.

episode: Trouble in China
headline: The Graf Spee is cornered
article: On 13 December three British cruisers, Exeter, Ajax and Achilles, caught the Admiral Graf Spee off the River Plate estuary. The German ship outgunned them and badly damaged Exeter, but she was hit too and put into neutral Montevideo for repairs. Under international law Uruguay allowed only a short stay. British diplomats spread rumours that a carrier and battlecruiser were waiting offshore. On 17 December Captain Hans Langsdorff took his ship out into the estuary and scuttled her in front of large crowds. He shot himself in Buenos Aires three days later. It was Britain's first naval victory of the war and was celebrated accordingly. In China, Nationalist armies were launching a winter offensive against Japanese positions that achieved little at heavy cost.

episode: Stalinʼs Unexpected Bedfellows - Soviet Relations in East Asia
headline: Moscow and Tokyo after Khalkhin Gol
article: Stalin's east was quieter than his west because of a battle few in Europe had followed. At Khalkhin Gol on the Mongolian–Manchurian border, Soviet and Mongolian forces under Georgy Zhukov had smashed a Japanese force in August 1939, in the same days the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact was signed. A ceasefire followed in September, and through the winter both governments negotiated border commissions and trade. The lesson in Tokyo was that the Red Army was dangerous, which strengthened those who argued for expansion south toward European colonies rather than north into Siberia. The lesson in Moscow was that Japan could be held. Zhukov's reputation was made. For now the USSR could concentrate on Finland, where its army was still struggling badly as the year ended.

episode: The Finns Strike Again and Japan Strikes Back
headline: The Raate road and a stubborn Japan
article: In the first week of January Finnish troops completed the destruction of the Soviet 44th Division on the Raate road near Suomussalmi. Several thousand Soviet soldiers were killed or froze; the Finns captured dozens of tanks and field guns they badly needed. The division's commander, Alexei Vinogradov, escaped but was shot on Stalin's orders for the defeat. In Asia, Japan's war in China ground on. Its armies held the coast, the major cities and the railways but could not force Chiang Kai-shek's government in Chongqing to surrender. Tokyo was now looking at Western supply routes to China, through French Indochina and British Burma, as the thing to cut. The Finnish victories made great headlines; the Red Army quietly began to reorganise for a different kind of attack.

episode: The Red Army Regroups to Crush Finland
headline: Timoshenko takes over in Finland
article: After a month of failure Stalin reorganised the Finnish front. Semyon Timoshenko took command of a new North-Western Front on 7 January with orders to break the Mannerheim Line properly. The Red Army paused major attacks, brought up heavy artillery and fresh divisions, and trained infantry to work with tanks and engineers against bunkers. Soviet bombers kept striking Finnish towns. Finland used the lull to rest troops but had no reserves worth the name and was running short of shells. Britain and France talked about sending an expedition to help Finland through northern Norway and Sweden, which would conveniently also cut Germany off from Swedish iron ore. Oslo and Stockholm, determined to stay neutral, made clear they would not allow it.

episode: Swedes not Sweden to Finland's Rescue
headline: Swedish volunteers, not Swedish troops
article: Sweden refused to join the war but did a great deal short of it. About 8,000 Swedish volunteers formed a corps that took over a sector of the front at Salla in Finnish Lapland, freeing Finnish units for the south. Sweden also sent aircraft, artillery, ammunition and money, and its pilots flew with the volunteer F 19 wing. Volunteers from Norway, Denmark, Hungary and elsewhere arrived in smaller numbers. Stockholm's priority was to avoid giving either Moscow or Berlin a reason to invade, and to keep the Allies off its soil. In the Gulf of Finland the ice froze hard enough for troops to cross, widening the front the Finns had to watch. Soviet bombers hit Finnish cities repeatedly through January.

episode: The Enigma of Germany's Wartime Economy
headline: Germany's war economy under strain
article: Germany had gone to war years earlier than its own planners wanted. Its economy was large but short of oil, rubber, copper and foreign currency, and the British blockade cut off most overseas trade. The regime leaned on the Soviet Union, which under a February 1940 trade agreement shipped grain, oil and metals in exchange for machinery and weapons technology, and on Swedish iron ore shipped through Narvik in winter. Göring's Four Year Plan office and the military competed for control of armaments. In March, Fritz Todt was made minister of armaments and munitions to bring some order. Rationing at home was already in force. The picture Allied planners drew was of a Germany that might be strangled slowly. It was too optimistic: Germany was about to gain the resources of half of Europe.

episode: The Soviet Hammer Strikes Hard at Finland
headline: The Soviet hammer falls on Summa
article: From the start of February the Red Army opened a sustained bombardment along the Mannerheim Line, firing hundreds of thousands of shells a day at selected sectors. On 1 February the main assault began, aimed especially at the Summa sector on the road to Viipuri. Infantry now advanced behind tanks, sledges carried armoured shields, and engineers blew bunkers with demolition charges. The Finns held for ten days of near-continuous fighting while their positions were smashed and their men worn down by lack of sleep. Mannerheim asked repeatedly for foreign troops; very few arrived. In London and Paris the plan for a Scandinavian expedition grew more concrete, though it still depended on Norwegian and Swedish permission that would never be given.

episode: Stalemate in China, Bombs over Finland
headline: Stalemate in China, bombs over Finland
article: In China the fighting had reached a grim balance. Japan's 1939–40 winter battles in Guangxi and along the Yangtze gained ground but could not finish Chiang Kai-shek's government, which had moved inland to Chongqing. Japanese bombers struck the city repeatedly in a campaign that killed thousands of civilians and would intensify through 1940. Communist forces under Mao Zedong held base areas in the north and fought a guerrilla war against Japan while also competing with the Nationalists for control. In Finland, Soviet bombers raided Helsinki, Viipuri, Turku and smaller towns, but the Finnish civilian death toll stayed relatively low thanks to shelters and dispersal. The main danger to Finland lay on the Karelian Isthmus, where the Mannerheim Line was beginning to crack.

episode: Finlandʼs Desperate Fight
headline: The Mannerheim Line is broken
article: On 11 February Soviet troops broke through at Lähde, near Summa, the decisive breach of the main Finnish defensive line. Mannerheim ordered a withdrawal to the intermediate and then rear lines closer to Viipuri, Finland's second city. The retreat was carried out in reasonable order, but the men were exhausted and shells were rationed. Finland's government, led by Risto Ryti with foreign minister Väinö Tanner, began exploring peace terms through Sweden. Stockholm told Helsinki plainly that Swedish troops would not come and that Finland should settle. The Allies, meanwhile, promised an expeditionary force of tens of thousands if Finland formally asked for it, an offer that Finnish leaders suspected was more about Narvik than about them.

episode: Manstein Makes a Plan and Hitler has a Man Crush
headline: Manstein's plan reaches Hitler
article: German plans for invading the West had originally been a cautious rerun of 1914: a sweep through central Belgium. After a German plane carrying parts of the plan crash-landed at Mechelen in January, the army looked again. Erich von Manstein, chief of staff of Army Group A, had argued for months that the main blow should come through the wooded Ardennes, cross the Meuse at Sedan, and race to the Channel, cutting off the Allied armies that would move into Belgium. His superiors found him tiresome and posted him to a corps command. On 17 February, over lunch, he got to explain the idea to Hitler directly. Hitler, who had been groping toward something similar, embraced it. In the Altmark incident the day before, British sailors had boarded a German supply ship in Norwegian waters and freed 299 prisoners.

episode: Hitler Plans His New Wars - Fall Gelb
headline: Fall Gelb takes its final shape
article: On 24 February the German army issued the revised directive for Fall Gelb, Case Yellow, built around Manstein's idea. Army Group B in the north would invade the Netherlands and Belgium loudly enough to draw the Allies forward. Army Group A, with most of the panzer divisions, would push through Luxembourg and the Ardennes, cross the Meuse and drive for the sea. Army Group C would hold the Maginot Line. Many generals thought the Ardennes too risky for tanks. In Allied headquarters the Dyle Plan stood: the best French armies and the British Expeditionary Force would move into Belgium the moment it was attacked. Each side's plan, in other words, fitted the other's almost perfectly, to Germany's advantage. In the north, Finland asked Moscow for terms.

episode: Finnish Winter is Almost Over
headline: Finland's last stand at Viipuri
article: In early March the Red Army attacked across the frozen Bay of Viipuri to outflank the city from the west, landing troops on the far shore. Finnish defenders, now with almost no reserves, held on by improvisation. Peace negotiations began in Moscow on 7 March, with Ryti leading the Finnish delegation. The Soviet terms were harsher than in autumn: all of the Karelian Isthmus including Viipuri, the shores of Lake Ladoga, a lease on Hanko, and territory in the north. Mannerheim told the government the army could not hold much longer. The Allies pressed Finland to keep fighting and ask for their expedition, which would not have arrived for weeks. Finland chose to negotiate.

episode: The Soviets Finish a Costly Winter War
headline: The Winter War ends
article: The Moscow Peace Treaty was signed on 12 March and the guns stopped at 11 a.m. the next day. Finland kept its independence but lost about 11 percent of its territory, including Viipuri. More than 400,000 Karelians, around a tenth of the population, chose to leave their homes rather than live under Soviet rule. Finland had lost about 25,000 dead. Soviet losses were far higher, at least 125,000 dead by later estimates. The Red Army had won, but its performance convinced foreign observers, Hitler included, that it was weak. In Paris, the failure to help Finland brought down Édouard Daladier's government; Paul Reynaud became prime minister on 21 March, promising a more aggressive war.

episode: Il Duce and der Führer Have a Date - The Axis War Plans
headline: Hitler and Mussolini meet at the Brenner
article: On 18 March Hitler and Mussolini met in a railway carriage at the Brenner Pass on the Austro-Italian border. Italy had declared "non-belligerence" in September 1939; its army was poorly equipped after wars in Ethiopia and Spain, and Mussolini had told Hitler Italy could not fight before 1942 or 1943. Now Hitler told him an offensive in the West was coming and invited Italy to join once it was clear how things were going. Mussolini, eager not to be left out of a German victory, promised he would enter the war at the right moment. In Britain, rationing of meat began, and the government planned how to stop Swedish iron ore reaching Germany along the Norwegian coast.

episode: Allies Plan to Hit the Nazis Where it Hurts
headline: The Allies plan to mine Norway's waters
article: At the Supreme War Council on 28 March Britain and France agreed to lay mines in Norwegian territorial waters to force German ore ships out to sea, where the Royal Navy could stop them. The plan, Operation Wilfred, was to be followed by landings at Narvik, Trondheim, Bergen and Stavanger if Germany reacted. The council also agreed that neither country would make a separate peace. French proposals to bomb Soviet oil fields in the Caucasus, which supplied Germany, were discussed and shelved. Allied planners assumed they had the initiative. In Berlin, German planning for an invasion of Denmark and Norway, Weserübung, was already complete and troopships were being loaded.

episode: Germans and British make their way to the North
headline: Two fleets head north
article: In the first week of April both sides were moving toward Norway. German supply ships disguised as merchantmen sailed for Norwegian ports from 3 April, and warships carrying troops left German harbours on the 6th and 7th. RAF reconnaissance spotted heavy German units moving north on 7 April, but the Admiralty assumed it was a breakout into the Atlantic and moved the Home Fleet to block that instead. British destroyers began laying Wilfred mines off Narvik on the morning of 8 April. That same day the destroyer Glowworm ran into the cruiser Admiral Hipper and rammed her before sinking. The Polish submarine Orzeł sank the German transport Rio de Janeiro off southern Norway; survivors told Norwegian rescuers they were going to Bergen.

episode: The Invasion of Norway and Denmark
headline: Germany seizes Denmark and invades Norway
photo: f:The German Invasion of Norway, 1940 N229.jpg
article: Before dawn on 9 April German forces occupied Denmark, which surrendered within hours, and landed in Norway at Oslo, Kristiansand, Bergen, Trondheim and Narvik. In the Oslofjord, the old guns and torpedoes of Oscarsborg fortress sank the new heavy cruiser Blücher, carrying troops and officials meant to take the capital. The delay let King Haakon VII, the government and the gold reserve escape north. Vidkun Quisling announced himself prime minister on the radio; the king refused to accept him. On 10 April and again on 13 April British destroyers attacked at Narvik and destroyed all ten German destroyers there. Norway had been caught by surprise, but it was fighting.

episode: The Scramble For Norway
headline: The scramble for Norway
article: Britain and France now improvised the landings they had planned. British troops went ashore at Harstad near Narvik from 14 April, and at Namsos and Åndalsnes to either side of Trondheim from 16 to 18 April, intending a pincer on the city. They were short of artillery, anti-aircraft guns, transport and maps, some units had their equipment loaded on the wrong ships, and German aircraft operating from captured airfields controlled the sky. Norwegian troops fought delaying actions in the valleys north of Oslo. German paratroopers dropped at Dombås were rounded up by Norwegians after several days. Neutral Sweden came under German pressure to allow transit of supplies and held out for now.

episode: Norway is Burning
headline: Norway burns
article: German columns pushed north from Oslo up the Gudbrandsdal and Østerdal valleys toward Trondheim, pushing Norwegian and newly arrived British troops back in a string of rearguard fights such as Kvam. The Luftwaffe bombed the small towns used as Allied ports, and Namsos, Åndalsnes, Molde and others were largely burned. British commanders reported that without air cover the positions south of Trondheim could not be held. In London the War Cabinet decided on 26–27 April to withdraw from central Norway and concentrate on Narvik. The campaign's handling, much of it directed by Churchill at the Admiralty, was becoming a political problem for Chamberlain.

episode: Retreat in Norway, Preparations in Western Europe
headline: Retreat from central Norway
article: Between 30 April and 3 May the Royal Navy evacuated Allied troops from Åndalsnes and Namsos. The Norwegian forces in the south, left behind, began to surrender. King Haakon and his government went north to Tromsø. Around Narvik, British, French, Polish and Norwegian troops continued to press the German mountain troops under General Dietl. In London the failure prompted the Norway Debate in the House of Commons on 7–8 May. The Conservative Leo Amery quoted Cromwell at Chamberlain: "In the name of God, go." The government won the vote but its majority fell from over 200 to 81. Across the Channel, German forces were massing on the borders of the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg.

episode: Hitler Strikes in the West - The Invasion of the Benelux
headline: Germany strikes in the West; Churchill takes over
article: At dawn on 10 May Germany invaded the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg. Glider-borne troops landed on top of Belgium's modern fort at Eben-Emael and disabled it within hours; paratroopers seized bridges around Rotterdam and Moerdijk. As planned, British and French armies drove into Belgium to meet the attack. The same evening Chamberlain resigned and King George VI asked Winston Churchill to form a coalition government. Churchill told the Commons on 13 May he had nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat. Meanwhile, largely unseen by Allied air reconnaissance, German armoured columns were crawling through the Ardennes toward the Meuse.

episode: Blitzkrieg in the West - The Invasion of France
headline: The breakthrough at Sedan
article: On 13 May German infantry crossed the Meuse at Sedan under a massive Luftwaffe bombardment that broke the nerve of second-rate French reserve divisions. Guderian's panzers were across the next day; Allied bombers attacking the bridges were shot down in large numbers. Further north Rommel's division crossed at Dinant. On 14 May the Luftwaffe bombed central Rotterdam, killing around 900 people, and the Netherlands surrendered the next day. On 15 May Reynaud telephoned Churchill: "We are beaten; we have lost the battle." Churchill flew to Paris the next day and found officials burning files. German armour was now racing west across open country behind the Allied armies in Belgium.

episode: The Allied Clusterf**k - The Battle of France
headline: The panzers reach the Channel
article: On 20 May German armour reached Abbeville at the mouth of the Somme, cutting the Allied armies in the north off from France. The French commander-in-chief, Gamelin, was sacked and replaced by the 73-year-old Maxime Weygand. A British counterattack at Arras on 21 May, with a few dozen tanks, shook Rommel's division badly and made German commanders nervous about their flanks, but it was too small to change anything. Weygand's plan to cut the panzer corridor from north and south never came together. Boulogne fell; Calais was ordered to hold to the end. On 24 May Hitler confirmed a halt order that stopped the panzers short of Dunkirk for three days. The British began planning to evacuate.

episode: The First Brexit? - The Dunkirk Evacuation
headline: Evacuation from Dunkirk
article: Operation Dynamo began on 26 May. Belgium's King Leopold III surrendered his army on 28 May, exposing the British flank. Over nine days, destroyers, ferries, minesweepers and hundreds of small civilian craft lifted about 338,000 British and French troops from the harbour mole and the beaches at Dunkirk, while French rearguards held the perimeter and the RAF fought over it at a distance. The army left behind almost all its tanks, guns and vehicles. Britain lost six destroyers and the French navy three. In London the War Cabinet argued over whether to explore peace terms through Mussolini; Churchill prevailed against Halifax. The evacuation was a deliverance and a defeat at the same time. Churchill said as much.

episode: Will Britain Remain?!
headline: Britain will fight on; France fights on the Somme
photo: w:We shall fight on the beaches
article: Dunkirk ended on 4 June with the last French troops taken off and some 40,000 left to surrender. That afternoon Churchill told the Commons "we shall fight on the beaches", a speech aimed as much at the United States as at Germany. On 5 June Germany launched Fall Rot, the second phase, against the French line along the Somme and Aisne. French divisions fought much harder than in May, using "hedgehog" defences in villages, but they were outnumbered and had no reserves. Norway's last fighting ended as the Allies evacuated Narvik, which they had captured on 28 May, and King Haakon left for London on 7 June.

episode: Britain Votes to Leave
headline: Italy enters the war; Paris falls
photo: s:Germans Paris June 1940 Arc de Triomphe
article: On 10 June, with France plainly beaten, Mussolini declared war on France and Britain. Roosevelt called it a stab in the back. The French government left Paris for Tours and then Bordeaux. Paris was declared an open city and German troops entered it unopposed on 14 June; a swastika flag went up on the Eiffel Tower. Verdun fell on the 15th. Reynaud wanted to fight on from North Africa; much of his cabinet, led by Marshal Pétain and Weygand, wanted an armistice. Churchill offered an "Anglo-French Union" with common citizenship, a measure of desperation. Reynaud resigned on 16 June, and Pétain formed a government to ask for terms.

episode: Nazi Europe?! - The Fall of France
headline: France signs an armistice
article: Pétain asked for terms on 17 June and told the French people by radio that the fighting must stop. The next day, from London, a little-known brigadier-general named Charles de Gaulle broadcast an appeal on the BBC for the French to continue the war. Hitler chose the place of signing for humiliation: the same railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne where Germany had signed the armistice of 1918. The armistice was signed there on 22 June and with Italy two days later. Germany would occupy the north and the whole Atlantic coast; a French government would run the unoccupied south and keep the empire and the fleet. France would pay for the occupation and its 1.5 million prisoners of war would stay in German camps.

episode: Paris - German Victory in France
headline: Hitler tours Paris; the Baltic states are swallowed
photo: f:Bundesarchiv Bild 183-H28708, Paris, Eiffelturm, Besuch Adolf Hitler.jpg
w:Soviet occupation of the Baltic states (1940)
article: Early on 23 June Hitler made a three-hour sightseeing tour of an empty Paris with his architect Albert Speer and the sculptor Arno Breker, posing in front of the Eiffel Tower and standing at Napoleon's tomb. He did not come back. The armistice came into force on 25 June. Stalin used Europe's distraction to collect the rest of his share: Soviet troops occupied Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia in mid-June, and on 28 June Romania was forced to hand over Bessarabia and northern Bukovina. Britain stood without allies in Europe apart from the exiled governments in London. Churchill's speech of 18 June had warned of the battle to come: "the Battle of France is over. I expect that the Battle of Britain is about to begin."

episode: Do the Brits hate the French?! - The Bombing of Mers-el-Kébir
headline: Britain fires on the French fleet
article: The armistice left France's powerful navy intact, and Churchill's government would not risk it falling into German hands. On 3 July a British force under Admiral Somerville arrived off Mers-el-Kébir in Algeria and gave the French squadron an ultimatum: join the British, sail to a British or distant neutral port, or scuttle. Negotiations failed, and that evening British battleships opened fire. The battleship Bretagne blew up and nearly 1,300 French sailors were killed. French ships in British ports were seized the same day, and those at Alexandria were disarmed by agreement. Vichy broke off relations with Britain. The attack shocked France. It also told the world, and especially Washington, that Britain intended to fight.

episode: The Dictator of France - The Rise of Philippe Pétain
headline: Pétain takes full power at Vichy
article: On 10 July the French National Assembly, meeting in the spa town of Vichy, voted 569 to 80 to give Marshal Pétain full powers to draw up a new constitution. The next day he made himself "Head of the French State", and the Third Republic was over. The new regime replaced "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" with "Work, Family, Fatherland" and set about blaming the defeat on parliamentarians, Freemasons, communists and Jews. Pierre Laval became its deputy leader. Most French people, stunned by defeat, gave the 84-year-old hero of Verdun the benefit of the doubt. In London, de Gaulle's Free French numbered only a few thousand. The Luftwaffe began attacking convoys in the Channel, the opening phase of the air battle.

episode: Good People on Both Sides? - Hitler's Peace Offer to the Allies
headline: Hitler offers peace; Britain refuses
article: On 19 July Hitler addressed the Reichstag, promoted a dozen generals to field marshal, and made what he called a final appeal to reason to Britain. He offered no actual terms, only the suggestion that Britain accept German domination of the continent. The British response came within an hour from a BBC journalist and officially on 22 July from Lord Halifax: no. Hitler had already issued Directive 16 on 16 July, ordering preparations for a landing in England, Operation Sea Lion, which would require the Luftwaffe to destroy the RAF first. Meanwhile Germany looked east: by late July Hitler was telling his generals that the USSR should be attacked in 1941.

episode: No Deal... Herr Hitler! - The Battle of Britain Begins
headline: The Battle of Britain begins over the Channel
article: Through July the Luftwaffe attacked coastal convoys and ports to draw RAF Fighter Command into battle over the Channel. The British counted 10 July as the start of the Battle of Britain. Fighter Command, under Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding, had about 600 serviceable Hurricanes and Spitfires and a system no other air force possessed: a chain of radar stations feeding plots to filter rooms and operations rooms, which directed squadrons by radio to intercept raids. Losses at sea mounted and the Admiralty pulled destroyers out of Dover in late July. The Luftwaffe was preparing its main assault, code-named Adlerangriff, Eagle Attack, against airfields and the radar chain.

episode: The Hippo vs. the Bulldog - The Battle of Britain Heats Up
headline: Fighter Command braces
article: The air fighting widened at the start of August, with raids on Channel shipping and coastal targets and growing losses on both sides. On 1 August Hitler issued Directive 17, ordering the Luftwaffe to overpower the RAF "in the shortest possible time". Göring believed it would take a few days. British aircraft production, driven by Lord Beaverbrook, was outpacing German production of fighters, but trained pilots were the real limit. Fighter Command drew in pilots from bomber and coastal units, the Fleet Air Arm, and squadrons of Poles, Czechs, Canadians and others who had escaped or volunteered. In Somaliland, Italian forces from Ethiopia were advancing on the small British garrison.

episode: Hail Mussolini, Haile Selassie's Usurper - The War in Somaliland
headline: Italy invades British Somaliland
article: On 3 August Italian forces from Ethiopia, which Mussolini had conquered in 1935–36, invaded British Somaliland on the Gulf of Aden with roughly 25,000 men against a British garrison of a few thousand Somali, Indian, African and British troops. The Italians outnumbered the defenders many times over in men, artillery and aircraft. The defenders made a stand at the Tug Argan gap on the road to the port of Berbera. Italy had over 250,000 troops in East Africa, though most were local colonial units and the colony was cut off from Italy by British control of Suez. Haile Selassie, the exiled Ethiopian emperor, was preparing to return to Sudan to lead resistance.

episode: Il Duce Kicks Churchill Where it Hurts - The British Lose Somaliland
headline: Britain abandons Somaliland; Eagle Day
article: After four days of fighting at Tug Argan, the British commander judged the position lost, and between 15 and 18 August about 7,000 troops and civilians were evacuated from Berbera to Aden. It was the only British colony Italy ever conquered. Churchill was furious at the small number of casualties, which he took to mean the position had not been properly defended. Over Britain the Luftwaffe launched Eagle Day on 13 August and on 15 August, the heaviest day of the campaign, attacked from Norway as well as France and lost heavily in the north. On 20 August Churchill told the Commons: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few."

episode: The Battle of Britain is a Bitch
headline: The airfields under attack
article: From 18 August the Luftwaffe concentrated on Fighter Command's airfields in south-east England. Kenley, Biggin Hill, Hornchurch, Manston and others were bombed repeatedly; ground crews, including women of the WAAF, kept them working under fire. 18 August, with heavy losses on both sides, became known as "the hardest day". Keith Park's 11 Group, defending the south-east, was stretched thin, and arguments raged with the neighbouring 12 Group over tactics. On the night of 24 August German bombers, apparently off course, dropped bombs on central London. Churchill ordered a retaliatory raid on Berlin the next night. It did little damage but enraged Hitler.

episode: 366 Days of Crushed Hopes, Suffering and Death
headline: One year of war
article: The war was a year old. Poland, Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France had fallen; the Baltic states and parts of Romania had been annexed by the USSR. Britain and its empire fought on with no ally but exile governments. The air battle was at its most dangerous in the last days of August, with Fighter Command losing pilots faster than training schools could replace them and sector stations badly damaged. On 30 August Romania was forced by the "Second Vienna Award" to cede northern Transylvania to Hungary. In the Atlantic, U-boats operating from new bases in occupied France were sinking ships at a rate that alarmed the Admiralty. The United States was edging toward Britain but was still neutral.

episode: Burn London, Burn - The Blitz Begins
headline: The Blitz begins
photo: f:Air Raid Damage in Britain during the Second World War HU36200.jpg
article: On the afternoon of 7 September some 350 German bombers with fighter escort attacked London's docks in the East End. Fires burned through the night and guided more bombers in after dark. About 430 civilians were killed that day. It was the start of 57 consecutive nights of bombing on the capital. The switch from airfields to London gave Fighter Command a reprieve when it needed one, and its airfields and pilots recovered. On 2 September Britain and the United States had announced the destroyers-for-bases deal: 50 old American destroyers in exchange for leases on British bases in the western hemisphere. The invasion alarm was raised in Britain with the code word "Cromwell" the night the Blitz began.

episode: The Nazi Invasion of Britain?! - Operation Sealion
headline: Invasion barges in the Channel ports
article: German invasion preparations were visible from the air: hundreds of river barges, tugs and transports had been gathered in ports from Antwerp to Le Havre. RAF Bomber Command attacked them night after night and sank or damaged a significant number. The German army wanted a broad landing across southern England; the navy, which had lost much of its destroyer strength in Norway, insisted it could only protect a narrow crossing and needed air superiority to do even that. The decision date kept slipping. The British prepared beach defences, roadblocks, pillboxes and the Home Guard, and removed signposts. Night raids on London grew heavier, and Londoners took shelter in the Underground.

episode: The Brits teach the Germans to bugger off!
headline: Battle of Britain Day
article: On Sunday 15 September the Luftwaffe sent two large daylight raids against London expecting to find Fighter Command finished. Instead Park and Leigh-Mallory met them with most of their squadrons, including 12 Group's "Big Wing". German bomber formations were broken up and scattered. The RAF claimed far more kills than the actual figure of around 60 German aircraft, against about 29 British losses, but the meaning was clear in Berlin. On 17 September Hitler postponed Sea Lion indefinitely. Britain marks 15 September as Battle of Britain Day. Daylight fighting continued into October, but the Luftwaffe was turning to night bombing of cities. On 13 September Italian forces in Libya invaded Egypt.

episode: An Axis of Evil is Complete - Japan Joins Italy and Germany
headline: Germany, Italy and Japan sign the Tripartite Pact
article: On 27 September Germany, Italy and Japan signed the Tripartite Pact in Berlin. Each promised to assist the others if attacked by a power not yet in the war, which in practice meant the United States. The pact recognised German and Italian leadership in Europe and Japan's in East Asia. Japan had just moved troops into northern French Indochina with Vichy's reluctant consent, to cut a supply route to China. Washington responded by banning the export of scrap iron and steel to Japan. In Dakar, a British and Free French attempt to rally French West Africa to de Gaulle ended in failure on 25 September after Vichy forces fired back, a blow to de Gaulle's standing.

episode: Hitler and the Art of the Deal - German Negotiations with Spain
headline: Hitler and Franco at Hendaye
article: Hitler hoped to bring Spain into the war and take Gibraltar, closing the western Mediterranean to Britain. Franco's price was high: large amounts of grain, fuel and weapons for a country ruined by its civil war, and much of French North Africa, which Hitler could not give without driving Vichy into the Allied camp. Throughout the autumn Spanish and German officials negotiated. On 4 October Hitler and Mussolini met again at the Brenner. On 23 October Hitler met Franco at Hendaye on the French–Spanish border and came away saying he would rather have teeth pulled than go through it again. Spain stayed out, though it remained friendly to the Axis. The London Blitz continued nightly.

episode: Itʼs Raining Bombs, Keep Calm and Carry On - Life During the Blitz
headline: Life under the Blitz
photo: w:Use of London Underground stations as air-raid shelters
article: By October London had been bombed every night for a month. Hundreds of thousands of people slept in Tube stations, crypts, railway arches and garden Anderson shelters; many more stayed in their beds and took their chances. Fire crews, wardens, rescue squads and nurses worked through every raid. The government at first discouraged use of the Underground and then gave in, adding bunks, toilets and refreshments. Censorship and morale propaganda kept up the image of cheerful defiance, which was partly true and partly not: there was fear, exhaustion, looting and anger at poor shelter provision in working-class districts. Bombing spread to Birmingham, Liverpool, Bristol and other cities.

episode: USA enters WW2 in 1940?!
headline: America registers for the draft
photo: w:Selective Training and Service Act of 1940
article: On 16 October some 16 million American men registered for the first peacetime draft in US history under the Selective Training and Service Act. On 29 October Secretary of War Henry Stimson, blindfolded, drew the first number from a fishbowl. Roosevelt was campaigning for an unprecedented third term against Wendell Willkie, and both men promised to keep American boys out of foreign wars. Yet the country was rearming and moving step by step toward Britain. American factories were taking British orders, and British purchasing missions were running out of dollars. In Europe, Hitler met Pétain at Montoire on 24 October and the word "collaboration" entered public use.

episode: Hitler is Disappointed by his Allies
headline: Montoire: Pétain shakes Hitler's hand
article: Hitler spent late October on a tour of Western Europe by train, trying to build a coalition against Britain. At Hendaye Franco gave him nothing definite. At Montoire on 24 October he met Pétain, who agreed in principle to "collaboration" without signing anything specific. The photograph of the two shaking hands was widely published and did great damage to Pétain's reputation over time. Hitler wanted Vichy to defend its African empire against the British and Free French. His travels showed the limits of his position: his would-be allies all had competing interests. Then, on his way back, he learned that Mussolini was about to invade Greece.

episode: Mussolini plays Hitler like a Fiddle - The Invasion of Greece
headline: Italy invades Greece
photo: f:Greek soldiers fighting in the Albanian front.jpg
article: Before dawn on 28 October the Italian ambassador in Athens handed Prime Minister Ioannis Metaxas an ultimatum demanding passage for Italian troops. Metaxas refused, a moment Greeks still mark as "Ochi Day". Italian forces from Albania attacked within hours. Mussolini had planned it without telling Hitler, partly to show he too could win quick victories. The invasion began in autumn rain in mountains with poor roads, and the Greek army, mobilised fast, stopped the Italians in the Pindus range. Britain sent RAF squadrons to Greece and occupied Crete, which gave it a base deep in the Mediterranean. Hitler was angry. Mussolini's war had opened the Balkans to the British.

episode: Britainʼs First Victory, Germany Plunders Europe & Mussoliniʼs Folly
headline: Roosevelt re-elected; the Greeks push back
article: On 5 November Roosevelt won a third term with 449 electoral votes, giving him freedom to help Britain more openly. In Greece, the Italian offensive was failing everywhere, and in mid-November the Greek army counterattacked, driving the Italians back into Albania. In occupied Europe the plunder was becoming systematic: France's occupation costs were set at 20 million Reichsmarks a day at an artificial exchange rate, and German agencies were buying, requisitioning and looting art, food and industrial goods. In the Atlantic, the armed merchant cruiser Jervis Bay was sunk on 5 November by the pocket battleship Admiral Scheer while defending her convoy; most of the merchant ships escaped.

episode: Britain shows Japan how to Attack Pearl Harbor - Battle of Taranto
headline: Swordfish strike at Taranto
article: On the night of 11–12 November, 21 Fairey Swordfish biplanes flew from the carrier Illustrious and attacked the Italian battle fleet in its harbour at Taranto. In two waves they torpedoed three battleships, sinking the Conte di Cavour and putting the Littorio and Caio Duilio out of action for months. Two aircraft were lost. In one night the balance of naval power in the Mediterranean shifted to Britain, and the Italian fleet moved north to Naples. Japanese naval officers studied the attack closely; it proved that aircraft could sink battleships in a shallow harbour with torpedoes. In Berlin, Molotov arrived for talks on 12 November.

episode: Cracks in the Soviet-Nazi Alliance
headline: Molotov in Berlin
article: Molotov's visit to Berlin on 12–13 November was supposed to explore Soviet membership of the Tripartite Pact. Hitler and Ribbentrop offered the USSR a vague sphere toward India and the Persian Gulf. Molotov asked precise questions about Finland, Romania, Bulgaria and the Turkish straits, areas where German and Soviet interests collided. During a British air raid the talks moved to a shelter, where Ribbentrop insisted Britain was finished; Molotov reportedly asked why, then, they were in a shelter. Stalin later sent written conditions that Hitler never answered. Hungary, Romania and Slovakia joined the Tripartite Pact in late November. Coventry was devastated by bombing on 14 November.

episode: The German Plan to Destroy French Culture - The Occupation of France
headline: The occupation of France settles in
photo: w:German occupation of France during World War II
article: Five months in, occupied France had a routine: German clocks, German road signs, a curfew, and a demarcation line between the zones that needed a pass to cross. Food was rationed and getting scarcer. The Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg was seizing art collections owned by Jews, with the Jeu de Paume museum used as a sorting depot. Vichy had already passed its own anti-Jewish statute in October, excluding Jews from public service and the professions without being asked. On 11 November students in Paris demonstrated at the Arc de Triomphe and were dispersed with arrests and shots. Resistance was still small and scattered, mostly leaflets and listening to the BBC.

episode: The Road to Moscow - German Invasion Plans
headline: Planning the road to Moscow
article: Through late autumn the German army staff worked on plans for invading the Soviet Union. General Marcks and General Paulus drafted and war-gamed variants; the army chief of staff Franz Halder favoured a main thrust on Moscow. On 5 December Halder briefed Hitler, who agreed in principle but wanted the Baltic and Ukraine taken as well, priorities that would never be fully settled. The planners assumed the Red Army would be destroyed near the border within weeks and that logistics would then be manageable. They seriously underestimated Soviet reserves. In Greece the Italians were in retreat; Pogradec and Gjirokastër fell to the Greeks in early December.

episode: The Empire Strikes Back - Britainʼs Operation Compass
headline: Operation Compass routs the Italians
article: On 9 December the British Western Desert Force under Richard O'Connor, about 36,000 men, attacked an Italian army several times its size that had dug in around Sidi Barrani in western Egypt. Planned as a five-day raid, it became a rout. Indian and British infantry with Matilda tanks overran the Italian fortified camps one after another, and some 38,000 prisoners were taken in the first days. The Italians fell back into Libya. In London the news came as a huge boost after months of bad news, and O'Connor was ordered to press on toward Bardia. In Washington, Roosevelt was considering how to keep supplies flowing to Britain once its dollars ran out.

episode: Red Beardʼs Ghost Returns - German Invasion Plans
headline: Directive 21: Barbarossa
article: On 18 December Hitler signed Directive 21, Operation Barbarossa: "The German Armed Forces must be prepared, even before the conclusion of the war against England, to crush Soviet Russia in a rapid campaign." Preparations were to be complete by 15 May 1941. Finland and Romania were expected to take part. The name came from Frederick Barbarossa, the medieval emperor said to sleep beneath a mountain until Germany needed him. On 17 December Roosevelt, at a press conference, compared aid to Britain to lending a neighbour a garden hose to put out a fire, the idea that became Lend-Lease. In Libya, O'Connor's troops had surrounded the Italian fortress of Bardia.

episode: Winter is Coming, Peace is Not - The Frozen Fronts
headline: A cold Christmas, a long war
article: The year closed with fronts frozen in place. In Albania, Greek and Italian troops fought in snow at high altitude; in Libya, O'Connor's forces prepared to storm Bardia. On 29 December Roosevelt gave a fireside chat calling the United States the "great arsenal of democracy". That night the Luftwaffe dropped incendiaries on the City of London, starting the "Second Great Fire". St Paul's Cathedral survived, and a photograph of its dome rising through the smoke became one of the defining images of the war. Britain had survived 1940. It had not won anything decisive, and the Germans controlled Europe from the North Cape to the Pyrenees.

episode: It's 1941 - A World at War
headline: Bardia falls
article: On 3 January the 6th Australian Division, in its first battle of the war, attacked the Italian fortress of Bardia just inside Libya with British tanks and artillery in support. In three days the garrison of some 40,000 surrendered. The Australians moved straight on to Tobruk. The year opened with the British empire winning in Africa while it was bombed at home and losing ships at sea. Roosevelt's State of the Union on 6 January set out the "Four Freedoms" — of speech, of worship, from want, from fear — as the aims a free world should defend. The Lend-Lease bill, titled "An Act to Further Promote the Defense of the United States", went to Congress on 10 January.

episode: Fighting Far Away From Home - Allied Advance in Africa
headline: Tobruk falls, and the empire fights far from home
article: Australian and British troops assaulted Tobruk on 21 January and took it the next day with another 25,000 prisoners and its valuable harbour. Meanwhile British and Indian forces pushed from Sudan into Italian-held Eritrea, and Haile Selassie crossed back into Ethiopia on 20 January with Gideon Force, a small unit of Ethiopian and Sudanese troops led by Orde Wingate. From Kenya, South African, East and West African troops prepared to invade Italian Somaliland. In early January the German Luftwaffe arrived in Sicily and attacked British shipping; the carrier Illustrious was badly damaged off Malta on 10 January. Germany was coming to Italy's rescue in the Mediterranean.

episode: Mao Against Everyone - China at War and Civil War
headline: China's war within a war
article: In the first weeks of January Nationalist troops ambushed and largely destroyed the headquarters of the communist New Fourth Army in southern Anhui as it moved north under orders from Chiang Kai-shek. Several thousand communist soldiers were killed or captured; the commander Ye Ting was imprisoned. The incident effectively ended the united front between the Nationalists and the Communists that had existed since 1937, though neither side formally renounced it. Both continued to fight Japan, but each also fought to position itself for the struggle that would follow. Japan held the coast and major cities but was bogged down. In Washington, China's supporters were lobbying for Lend-Lease aid to include Chongqing.

episode: When Anti-Semites Infight, Jews Still Die - Pogroms in Romania
headline: The Legionary rebellion and the Bucharest pogrom
article: On 21 January members of Romania's fascist Iron Guard, the Legion, rose against their partner in government, General Ion Antonescu. During three days of revolt, legionnaires attacked the Jewish districts of Bucharest. Around 125 Jews were murdered, many in horrific circumstances, synagogues were burned and Jewish homes and shops were looted. Antonescu put down the rebellion with the army, with Hitler's approval: Berlin preferred a reliable general to unstable street fascists. The legionaries' leaders fled to Germany. Antonescu's regime that followed was no protection to Romania's Jews. Within months, after the invasion of the USSR, Romanian forces would carry out massacres in Iași, Bessarabia and Transnistria in which hundreds of thousands of Jews were killed. This entry is shown without map styling.

episode: Africa, the Axisʼ Achilles Heel - The Allied African Campaigns
headline: Africa, the Axis weak point
article: By the end of January Italy's African empire was cracking on several fronts. In Libya, Australian and British troops took Derna on 30 January and pushed on toward Benghazi. In Eritrea, British and Indian troops reached the mountain fortress of Keren, where the Italians made their most determined stand of the East African campaign; the battle would last until late March. In southern Ethiopia, Kenya-based forces probed the frontier. Italy could not reinforce any of these armies because Britain controlled Suez and the Mediterranean sea lanes were dangerous. Mussolini's prestige was collapsing. In Berlin, Hitler agreed to send a small armoured force to Libya to stop the rot.

episode: Rommel to fix the Bungle in Benghazi
headline: Beda Fomm: an Italian army destroyed
article: As the Italian Tenth Army retreated along the coast road from Benghazi, O'Connor sent a small force of armour and motorised infantry straight across the desert to cut it off. On 5 February "Combe Force" reached the road at Beda Fomm, south of Benghazi, just ahead of the Italian columns. In two days of desperate fighting the Italians failed to break through, and on 7 February the remnants surrendered. In two months O'Connor's force of at most two divisions had advanced 800 kilometres and taken around 130,000 prisoners. O'Connor wanted to push to Tripoli. London stopped him: troops were needed for Greece. On 6 February Erwin Rommel was appointed to command the German force bound for Libya.

episode: Enter Erwin Rommel - The British Advance in Africa
headline: Rommel lands in Tripoli
article: Rommel flew to Tripoli on 12 February, and the first units of what would become the Deutsches Afrikakorps began unloading two days later. Officially he was subordinate to the Italian command and his orders were defensive: block any British advance to Tripoli. He immediately pushed his units forward toward the British positions at El Agheila, far beyond what his superiors had in mind, and paraded tanks through Tripoli repeatedly to inflate their apparent numbers. Facing him were tired, scattered British units whose best formations had been withdrawn for Greece or sent to refit. In East Africa, British forces took Kismayu in Italian Somaliland on 14 February.

episode: The Brits Will Walk 500 Miles, and They Will Walk 500 More
headline: The long march through Italian East Africa
article: From Kenya, General Alan Cunningham's force of South African, East African, West African and Gold Coast troops swept north-east through Italian Somaliland. Mogadishu fell on 25 February, and his columns then turned inland toward Ethiopia, covering more than 1,000 kilometres in a few weeks against crumbling resistance. Nigerian and Gold Coast units led much of the advance. In Ethiopia, patriot forces were growing as Haile Selassie moved toward his capital. The Italian commander, the Duke of Aosta, was cut off from reinforcement and short of fuel and ammunition. It was one of the fastest advances of the war and is little remembered outside the countries whose men made it.

episode: The Nazis Building Bridges, Not Walls
headline: German engineers bridge the Danube
article: In late February German engineers prepared pontoon bridges across the Danube from Romania into Bulgaria, ready for the Wehrmacht to cross as soon as Sofia agreed. Hitler had decided to rescue Mussolini in Greece and secure his southern flank before attacking the USSR; he also wanted to keep British bombers in Greece away from the Romanian oil fields at Ploiești. Bulgaria's King Boris was reluctant but surrounded by German power and tempted by the chance to recover territory lost in 1919. Turkey signed a non-aggression declaration with Bulgaria, signalling it would not intervene. In London the decision was taken to send British, Australian and New Zealand troops to Greece.

episode: Bulgaria Joins the Fascist Alliance
headline: Bulgaria joins the Axis
article: On 1 March Bulgaria signed the Tripartite Pact in Vienna, and German troops crossed the Danube the next day and moved toward the Greek border. Britain broke off relations with Sofia. On 4 March British commandos raided the Lofoten Islands in Norway, destroying fish-oil plants and capturing rotor wheels for an Enigma machine. The first British, Australian and New Zealand troops began landing in Greece on 7 March as part of "Lustre Force". The Greek government had accepted them knowing it might provoke Germany. In Libya, the British command assumed Rommel would not be ready to attack until May. It was badly wrong.

episode: Nigerians Chasing Italians Like Cheetahs Hunt a Bull
headline: The Nigerian advance and Lend-Lease
article: On 11 March Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act, letting the United States lend, lease or give war materials to any country whose defence it judged vital to American security. Britain no longer had to pay in dollars it did not have. It was the end of American neutrality in all but name. In East Africa, Nigerian troops of Cunningham's force advanced at extraordinary speed from Somaliland into Ethiopia, reaching Jijiga on 17 March and then Harar. British forces from Aden retook Berbera on 16 March. At Keren in Eritrea, the battle for the heights continued with heavy losses on both sides. The Italian empire in Africa had weeks left.

episode: Culling the Nazi Wolfpacks - Submarines, Spies, China, and Africa
headline: The U-boat aces fall
article: In one week in March the Royal Navy killed or captured three of Germany's most famous U-boat commanders. On 7 March Günther Prien, who had sunk the Royal Oak, was lost with U-47. On 17 March, while attacking convoy HX 112, Joachim Schepke's U-100 was rammed by HMS Vanoc, and Otto Kretschmer's U-99, the top-scoring boat, was forced to the surface and scuttled; Kretschmer was captured. It suggested escorts with better training and radar could hurt the wolf packs. Losses of merchant ships remained very high. Britain now also had a new Western Approaches command in Liverpool. Elsewhere: Japanese troops pushed in China, and in Africa the British closed on Keren and Harar.

episode: Yugoslavia Joins the Axis Powers. and then they donʼt
headline: Yugoslavia joins the Axis — then doesn't
article: Under heavy pressure, Yugoslavia's regent Prince Paul signed the Tripartite Pact in Vienna on 25 March. Two days later, a group of Serbian air force officers led by General Dušan Simović overthrew the government in a nearly bloodless coup, declared the 17-year-old Peter II of age, and crowds in Belgrade demonstrated against Germany. The new government tried to avoid war and did not formally repudiate the pact, but Hitler took it as a personal insult. He ordered that Yugoslavia be destroyed "militarily and as a state". The invasion of the USSR was pushed back to fit in a Balkan campaign. On 28 March the Royal Navy defeated the Italian fleet at Cape Matapan off Greece.

episode: Rommel Storms Into North-Africa
headline: Rommel attacks
article: On 31 March Rommel attacked the British positions at Mersa Brega, ahead of his orders and ahead of his superiors' expectations. The thin British front collapsed. Benghazi was abandoned on 3–4 April. Rommel split his forces into columns and sent them across the desert bulge of Cyrenaica toward the coast road, aiming to cut off the British. In the confusion O'Connor, sent forward to advise, was captured on 7 April. Almost everything won in the winter was lost in under two weeks. The Australians fell back into Tobruk. In Iraq, on 1 April, the pro-Axis Rashid Ali al-Gaylani seized power in Baghdad in a coup.

episode: Nazis in the Balkans - The Invasion of Greece and Yugoslavia
headline: Germany invades Yugoslavia and Greece
photo: f:Bundesarchiv Bild 101I-185-0117-02A, Griechenland, Panzer in Ort.jpg
article: On 6 April Germany attacked Yugoslavia and Greece at once. The Luftwaffe bombed Belgrade in Operation Punishment, killing thousands of civilians. German, Italian and Hungarian forces invaded Yugoslavia from several directions, and its army, spread thin along long frontiers and divided by national tensions, fell apart quickly. In Greece, German armour broke through the Metaxas Line forts and swung through southern Yugoslavia to outflank the main Greek and British positions. Salonika fell on 9 April. On 10 April a Croatian fascist state was proclaimed in Zagreb under the Ustaše, which would soon launch genocidal violence against Serbs, Jews and Roma. In Libya, Rommel surrounded Tobruk.

episode: Yugoslavia Crushed - Battle for Greece Continues
headline: Yugoslavia crushed; Tobruk holds
article: The Royal Yugoslav Army capitulated on 17 April, eleven days after the invasion began. King Peter and the government fled to London. In Greece, British and Commonwealth troops fell back from Mount Olympus to new positions as German armour pressed south. In Libya, Rommel's first attacks on Tobruk on 11–14 April were beaten back by the Australian 9th Division and British artillery. Tobruk was now besieged, supplied by sea from Alexandria at a heavy cost in ships. Its defenders, mocked by German propaganda as rats in a trap, adopted the name "Rats of Tobruk". In Asia, Japan and the Soviet Union signed a neutrality pact on 13 April.

episode: Another Last Stand at Thermopylae - The Battle of Greece
headline: A rearguard at Thermopylae
article: As Greek resistance collapsed in the north, Australian and New Zealand troops fought a rearguard at the historic pass of Thermopylae on 24–25 April to cover the withdrawal to the southern ports. The Greek army in Epirus, facing Germans behind it and Italians in front, capitulated on 20 April; its commander surrendered without government authority. Prime Minister Alexandros Koryzis killed himself on 18 April. The British began evacuating by sea on 24 April, mostly at night from small beaches in Attica and the Peloponnese. In Iraq, British troops landed at Basra on 18 April under Britain's treaty rights while relations with Rashid Ali's government deteriorated.

episode: Balkans in Nazi Hands - A Greek Tragedy
headline: Greece falls
article: German troops entered Athens on 27 April and raised the swastika over the Acropolis. The evacuation of the British, Australian and New Zealand force ended around 30 April; about 50,000 men were taken off, but thousands were captured and almost all heavy equipment was lost. Many evacuated troops went to Crete. Greece was divided into German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation zones and a famine began within months; tens of thousands died in Athens alone in the winter of 1941–42. On 30 April Rommel's renewed assault on Tobruk was repulsed. In Iraq, Rashid Ali's forces surrounded the RAF base at Habbaniya.

episode: Enigma Captured!
headline: Enigma captured from U-110
article: On 9 May the British destroyer Bulldog and other escorts forced U-110 to the surface after an attack on convoy OB 318. A boarding party under Sub-Lieutenant David Balme went into the sinking submarine and brought out its Enigma machine, codebooks and settings documents before it went down under tow. The capture was kept secret for decades; the crew were held apart so they would not report it. Combined with other captures that spring, it helped the codebreakers at Bletchley Park read U-boat signals for much of the rest of 1941, letting the Admiralty route convoys around wolf packs. In Iraq, British forces broke the siege of Habbaniya.

episode: Nazi Nuts Trading Places & Victory for the Commonwealth
headline: Rudolf Hess flies to Scotland
article: On the evening of 10 May Rudolf Hess, Hitler's deputy in the Nazi party, flew a Messerschmitt 110 alone from Augsburg to Scotland and parachuted near Eaglesham, apparently hoping to negotiate peace through the Duke of Hamilton. He was arrested and held for the rest of the war. Berlin declared him mentally disturbed; the British said very little, which fed Soviet suspicion for decades. The same night the Luftwaffe made its last major raid of the Blitz on London, killing about 1,400 people and damaging the Commons chamber. In East Africa, the Duke of Aosta's forces at Amba Alagi were surrounded and would surrender on 19 May.

episode: Invasion of Crete: a Bloody Mess
headline: Paratroopers over Crete
article: On 20 May Germany launched the first major airborne invasion in history against Crete, dropping thousands of paratroopers on the airfields at Maleme, Rethymno and Heraklion. Losses were appalling on the first day. Allied commanders, who had been warned via Ultra intelligence, were focused on a seaborne landing and failed to retake Maleme airfield, and the Germans flew in reinforcements. Cretan civilians joined the fighting. At sea, the Luftwaffe sank the cruisers Gloucester and Fiji and several destroyers trying to stop sea convoys. Out in the Atlantic, the battleship Bismarck had broken out, and on 24 May she sank the battlecruiser Hood.

episode: Sink the Bismarck! - The Pride of the Kriegsmarine's Demise
headline: The Hood lost, the Bismarck sunk
article: On 24 May in the Denmark Strait the Bismarck and Prinz Eugen met HMS Hood and the new battleship Prince of Wales. A shell from Bismarck hit Hood's magazines and she blew up; three of her 1,418 men survived. Bismarck, damaged, headed for France. The Royal Navy threw every available ship into the hunt. On 26 May Swordfish from the carrier Ark Royal jammed her rudder with a torpedo. The next morning the battleships Rodney and King George V reduced her to a wreck and she sank; over 2,000 German sailors died. On Crete, the British began evacuating on 28 May. In Iraq, Rashid Ali fled.

episode: British Officers Abandon Their Men to the Nazis
headline: Left behind on Crete
article: The evacuation of Crete ended on 1 June. About 16,000 British, Australian and New Zealand troops were lifted from the small south-coast port of Sphakia and from Heraklion, at a heavy cost in warships to German bombing. Roughly 12,000 were left behind and became prisoners; some escaped into the mountains, helped by Cretans who paid heavily in reprisals. Accounts of officers being taken off while their men waited on the beach caused bitterness that lasted for decades. German paratroop losses had been so severe that Hitler never again used them in a large airborne operation. In Iraq, Rashid Ali's regime collapsed; in Baghdad on 1–2 June, the Farhud pogrom killed some 180 Jews.

episode: Finland and France Join Hitler
headline: Finland drifts toward Germany; Syria invaded
article: Finland, still smarting from the Winter War, had been drawn into Barbarossa planning. German troops were already in Finnish Lapland, and in early June Finnish officers coordinated mobilisation dates with Berlin, though Helsinki would insist it fought a separate "Continuation War". On 8 June British, Australian, Indian and Free French forces invaded Vichy-held Syria and Lebanon, after Vichy had allowed German aircraft to use Syrian airfields during the Iraq revolt. Vichy troops fought hard. Free French soldiers were now fighting French soldiers loyal to Pétain. In Libya, Wavell prepared Operation Battleaxe to relieve Tobruk, using tanks rushed across the Mediterranean.

episode: French Killing French in Syria
headline: French against French in Syria
article: In Syria and Lebanon the fighting was bitter. Australian troops advancing up the coast met determined Vichy resistance at the Litani River and Damour; Free French and Indian troops fought toward Damascus, which fell on 21 June. In Libya, Operation Battleaxe, launched on 15 June, failed within three days: British tanks charged into German anti-tank screens, including the 88mm guns at Halfaya Pass, and lost heavily. Churchill replaced Wavell with Claude Auchinleck. Along the Soviet border, German, Romanian and Finnish forces had completed their deployment; Soviet intelligence and foreign governments had warned Stalin repeatedly. He dismissed the warnings as provocation.

episode: Operation Barbarossa - Biggest Land Invasion in History
headline: Operation Barbarossa begins
article: At about 3:15 a.m. on 22 June more than three million German troops, with Romanian and later Finnish, Hungarian, Slovak and Italian forces, attacked the Soviet Union along a front from the Baltic to the Black Sea. It was the largest invasion in history. The Luftwaffe destroyed well over a thousand Soviet aircraft on the ground on the first day. Soviet forward units, which had been ordered not to provoke the Germans, were overrun; communications collapsed. The garrison of the fortress at Brest held out for weeks behind the front. Molotov, not Stalin, broadcast the news to the Soviet people at noon. That night Churchill pledged British help to the USSR.

episode: Operation Barbarossa - End of the Nazi-Soviet Alliance
headline: The first great encirclements
article: Within a week German armoured groups had driven deep into Soviet territory. In the centre, Guderian's and Hoth's panzer groups closed a vast pocket around Białystok and Minsk; Minsk fell on 28 June, and over 300,000 Soviet soldiers would be captured. In the north, German troops reached Riga and the Dvina. In Ukraine, Soviet mechanised corps counterattacked around Dubno and Brody in one of the largest tank battles of the war, slowing Army Group South at enormous cost. Hungary and Slovakia declared war on the USSR; Finland joined on 25–26 June. In the occupied areas, SS Einsatzgruppen began mass shootings of Jews, communists and others behind the front.

episode: Wehrmacht 1/3 of Way to Moscow
headline: A third of the way to Moscow
article: By early July Army Group Centre had crossed the Berezina and was approaching the Dnieper and Smolensk, some 600 kilometres from the border and 400 from Moscow. On 3 July Stalin finally spoke to the Soviet people by radio, addressing them as "brothers and sisters" and calling for a scorched-earth retreat and partisan war. The State Defence Committee had been created under his chairmanship. Factories in the west were being dismantled and shipped east by rail, an evacuation that would eventually move some 1,500 enterprises to the Urals and Siberia. German commanders were triumphant. Halder wrote in his diary that the campaign had probably been won in fourteen days.

episode: Has Germany Lost WW2 Already in Mid-1941?
headline: Has Germany already lost?
article: The victories were huge, but so were the problems.
