German infantry divisions marched on foot behind the panzers and fell far behind; most supplies moved by horse-drawn cart on dirt roads; Soviet railways used a different gauge and had to be converted. Tank strength in the panzer divisions was dropping fast from breakdowns and losses. Soviet resistance, while chaotic, did not collapse: new armies appeared faster than German intelligence expected, and they counterattacked. At Smolensk, the encirclement battle that began around 10 July would take weeks. Some German officers privately began to wonder whether this would be a quick campaign after all. In London, Britain and the USSR signed a mutual assistance agreement on 12 July.

episode: Barbarossa: a Wehrmacht Soap Opera
headline: Barbarossa loses its shape
article: German troops took most of Smolensk on 16 July, but closing the pocket east of the city proved slow and costly, and large numbers of Soviet troops broke out. Hitler and the army leadership argued over what to do next. Hitler's Directive 33 of 19 July shifted panzer forces away from Moscow toward Leningrad in the north and Ukraine in the south, while Halder and the army group commanders wanted to keep driving for the capital. The argument would run for weeks while the panzer groups halted to refit. Japan, meanwhile, decided to move into southern Indochina. In the Baltic, German forces were closing on Estonia.

episode: The Wehrmacht - an Army on Horseback
headline: An army that marched on foot
article: Behind the panzer spearheads the Wehrmacht of 1941 looked much like the army of 1914. It used around 600,000 horses in the invasion of the USSR, pulling artillery, supply wagons and field kitchens. Most of its infantry walked, often 30 to 40 kilometres a day in summer heat and dust. Motor vehicles were a mixture of German and captured French, British and Czech types, which made spare parts a nightmare. The dirt roads of the western USSR turned into dust clouds in summer and mud in rain. The Soviets were in a similar position, but they were falling back toward their supplies while the Germans moved away from theirs. Soviet aircraft bombed Moscow's attackers; Moscow itself was bombed for the first time on 21–22 July.

episode: Japan is Getting Hungry, Barbarossa is Confused
headline: Japan moves south; Barbarossa argues with itself
article: On 24 July Vichy France agreed to let Japan station troops in southern Indochina, and they moved in over the following days, putting Japanese bombers within range of Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies. On 26 July Roosevelt froze Japanese assets in the United States; Britain and the Netherlands followed. On 1 August Washington stopped oil exports to Japan, which imported most of its oil from America. Tokyo's leaders now faced a choice between backing down in China or seizing the oil of the East Indies. In the USSR, the Smolensk pocket was finally mopped up, and German commanders still argued over Moscow.

episode: Tanks, but no Tanks - Hitler Hinders the Blitzkrieg
headline: Hitler turns the panzers south
article: In early August Army Group South closed a pocket around Uman in central Ukraine, capturing over 100,000 Soviet troops. Further north, Guderian's panzer group fought off Soviet counterattacks around Roslavl and Yelnya. Hitler's decision was becoming clear: he wanted the industrial and agricultural wealth of Ukraine and the Donbas, and the Soviet armies around Kiev, before Moscow. Guderian flew to the Wolf's Lair on 23 August to argue for Moscow and came away agreeing to lead his panzers south. Soviet production was meanwhile being relocated eastward; the Germans had underestimated how many tanks the USSR could build, and how fast it could replace lost armies.

episode: Churchill and Roosevelt vow to destroy all Nazis
headline: The Atlantic Charter
photo: s:Churchill Roosevelt Prince of Wales 1941 church service
article: Churchill and Roosevelt met for the first time as leaders aboard warships in Placentia Bay, Newfoundland, from 9 to 12 August. They issued a joint statement, the Atlantic Charter, setting out shared aims: no territorial gains, self-determination for peoples, freer trade, and a peace that would let all nations live in safety after "the final destruction of the Nazi tyranny". The United States was not at war, but its president had just signed a declaration of war aims with a belligerent. The phrase on self-determination would be quoted back at Britain for years by colonial nationalists. On Sunday 10 August the two leaders attended a church service on the deck of HMS Prince of Wales.

episode: "There are no Soviet Prisoners of War, only Traitors"
headline: The fate of Soviet prisoners
photo: w:German mistreatment of Soviet prisoners of war
article: In August 1941 Stalin issued Order No. 270, which declared Red Army soldiers who surrendered to be traitors and allowed the families of captured officers to be arrested. Millions were being captured. On the German side, Soviet prisoners were held in open-air enclosures with little or no food, shelter or medical care, and the regime deliberately excluded them from the protection given to Western prisoners. By the spring of 1942 around two million of them had died, and the total by 1945 was about three million, more than half of all those taken. Political commissars and Jewish prisoners were singled out and shot under the "Commissar Order". It was one of the largest crimes of the war and received relatively little attention afterwards.

episode: The Allies Invade Iran, Barbarossa Continues
headline: Britain and the USSR invade Iran
article: On 25 August British and Soviet forces invaded Iran from the south and north. They wanted to secure its oil fields and the Abadan refinery, expel German agents, and open a supply route to the USSR through the Persian Gulf. The Iranian army resisted for a few days. Reza Shah, who had been friendly with Germany, abdicated in favour of his son Mohammad Reza Pahlavi on 16 September. The Persian Corridor would carry a large share of Lend-Lease supplies to the Soviets. In Ukraine, Guderian's panzers turned south behind the Soviet armies defending Kiev, while Army Group North approached Leningrad.

episode: The war is two years old
headline: Two years of war; Leningrad is cut off
article: The war was two years old. Germany ruled continental Europe and its armies were deep in the Soviet Union. On 30 August German troops reached Mga, cutting the last railway linking Leningrad to the rest of the country, and on 8 September they took Shlisselburg on Lake Ladoga, completing the land blockade of the city. Finland's army had advanced to near the old 1939 border north of the city but would not attack it. About 2.5 million civilians were trapped. Hitler ordered that Leningrad be starved rather than stormed. The siege would last 872 days. In Britain, the convoy routes to Arkhangelsk began: the first Arctic convoy, "Dervish", arrived on 31 August.

episode: Victory for the Red Army!
headline: The Red Army retakes Yelnya
article: On 6 September Soviet troops under Zhukov retook the salient around Yelnya, east of Smolensk, which the Germans had held since July. It was the first time in the war that the Red Army had forced the Wehrmacht to give up ground in a planned operation, and Soviet propaganda made the most of it. Several rifle divisions were awarded the new title of "Guards". The victory came at heavy cost and was small next to the disaster forming in Ukraine, where Guderian's panzers from the north and Kleist's from the south were closing around Kiev. Stalin refused to allow the Kiev armies to withdraw.

episode: Another week, another half million for the Germans
headline: The Kiev pocket
article: On 14–15 September Guderian's and Kleist's panzer groups met near Lokhvytsia, 200 kilometres east of Kiev, closing the largest encirclement in military history. Stalin had refused repeated requests to withdraw; the commander of the South-Western Front, Kirponos, was killed trying to break out. Kiev fell on 19 September. The Germans claimed over 600,000 prisoners. It was a catastrophic Soviet defeat. It had also cost the Germans weeks of time, and the panzers now had to turn north again to strike at Moscow before the autumn rains. In the north, Zhukov had been sent to Leningrad to stiffen its defence, which he did with threats as much as tactics.

episode: Free from the Nazi Occupation - but for how long can it last? WW2
headline: Partisans and the promise of liberation
article: Some people in the Baltic states and western Ukraine, who had suffered Soviet deportations only months earlier, greeted the Germans as liberators. Ukrainian nationalists proclaimed an independent state in Lviv on 30 June; its leaders were promptly arrested by the Germans. Nazi plans had no room for independent states in the east, only colonies to be exploited and emptied. Behind German lines, Soviet partisan groups were forming, at first weak and poorly organised, often made up of soldiers cut off in the encirclements. Collective farms were kept going under German management because they made grain easier to seize. Around 26 September German forces near Kiev massacred more than 33,000 Jews at Babi Yar.

episode: A Huge New German Offensive Begins - Operation Typhoon!
headline: Operation Typhoon: the drive on Moscow
article: On 30 September Guderian's panzers attacked in the south, and on 2 October the main body of Army Group Centre launched Operation Typhoon, the offensive meant to take Moscow before winter. Hitler told the German people on 3 October that the enemy was broken and would never rise again. The Soviet defences, again poorly placed, collapsed. In the north Moscow conference of 29 September to 1 October, Britain and the US had agreed to send the USSR large monthly quantities of aircraft, tanks and raw materials. Roosevelt extended Lend-Lease to the Soviets in November. In the Atlantic, US Navy destroyers were now escorting convoys part of the way.

episode: An Open Road to Moscow!
headline: Vyazma and Bryansk: the road to Moscow opens
article: In the first week of October German armour closed two huge pockets around Vyazma and Bryansk, trapping much of the Soviet Western, Reserve and Bryansk Fronts. Around 600,000 to 700,000 Soviet soldiers were captured. For several days there was almost nothing standing between Army Group Centre and Moscow. Stalin recalled Zhukov from Leningrad on 6 October and put him in charge of the Moscow front, scraping together whatever he could along the Mozhaisk line. On 6–7 October the first snow fell, followed by rain. The roads began to turn into the deep mud of the rasputitsa, the season of bad roads.

episode: Panic in Moscow! The Germans are here!
headline: Panic in Moscow
article: On 15 October the Soviet government ordered the evacuation of ministries, foreign embassies and much of the party apparatus to Kuibyshev on the Volga. The next day Moscow panicked. Factories stopped, officials fled with their families, shops were looted and crowds besieged the railway stations. Lenin's body had already been moved to Siberia. Stalin stayed in the Kremlin. The NKVD restored order with arrests and shootings. Kaluga and Kalinin fell, and the Germans took Mozhaisk on 18 October. But the mud was now deep, German supply columns were stuck, and Soviet resistance in front of the capital was stiffening day by day.

episode: Martial Law in Moscow, but is the Cavalry coming?
headline: A state of siege in Moscow
article: On 19 October Stalin declared a state of siege in Moscow. Hundreds of thousands of civilians, most of them women, dug anti-tank ditches and trenches around the city. Militia divisions of factory workers and students were thrown into the line with little training. Fresh divisions were beginning to arrive from Siberia and the Far East, released after the spy Richard Sorge in Tokyo reported that Japan intended to strike south rather than north; Stalin had other sources too. In the south, German forces took Kharkov on 24 October and broke into Crimea, laying siege to Sevastopol. The German advance on Moscow had slowed to a crawl in the mud.

episode: Winter is Coming
headline: The mud stops the Wehrmacht
article: By the end of October the mud had brought Typhoon to a halt. Vehicles sank to their axles; tanks used up fuel at several times the normal rate; horses died in harness. Guderian's attempt to take Tula, the arms-making city south of Moscow, failed against its defenders. The Germans paused to bring up fuel and ammunition and to wait for the ground to freeze. The lull let Zhukov rebuild the Moscow defences. Winter clothing for the Wehrmacht was still mostly in depots in Poland; the army had planned for victory before winter. In the Atlantic, a U-boat sank the US destroyer Reuben James on 31 October, killing over a hundred American sailors.

episode: The Red Army must double in size... and now!
headline: The parade on Red Square
article: On 7 November, the anniversary of the revolution, Stalin held the traditional military parade on Red Square, with troops marching past the Kremlin walls and straight on to the front, some 70 kilometres away. Snow fell during the parade. The night before, in a speech held in the Mayakovskaya metro station, he had declared that if the Germans wanted a war of extermination, they would get one. Newsreels of the parade went around the world as proof that Moscow still stood. The Red Army had lost several million men in five months, and Stalin was ordering a vast mobilisation to replace them, conscripting older men and training new divisions in the east.

episode: Night Vision Brings Triumph to the British!
headline: Radar and Ultra sink an Axis convoy
article: On the night of 8–9 November Force K, two cruisers and two destroyers based at Malta, used radar to find and destroy an entire Italian convoy carrying supplies to Rommel, the "Duisburg convoy", without loss. The intelligence on its route came from decrypted Axis signals. Through the autumn British submarines, aircraft and ships from Malta sank a large share of Axis cargo headed for Libya, starving Rommel's forces of fuel just as the British prepared a new offensive. The Germans responded by sending U-boats into the Mediterranean and transferring a Luftwaffe air corps from Russia to Sicily. On 13 November a U-boat sank the carrier Ark Royal near Gibraltar.

episode: Surprise Attack On Rommel! - Operation Crusader Begins
headline: Operation Crusader begins
article: On 18 November the newly named British Eighth Army, under Alan Cunningham, launched Operation Crusader to destroy Rommel's armour and relieve Tobruk. It was the largest British offensive of the war so far, with over 700 tanks. The tank battles around the airfield at Sidi Rezegh, south-east of Tobruk, were chaotic and swung back and forth. British armour was committed piecemeal and suffered heavily against German anti-tank guns. On the night before the offensive, a British commando raid aimed at killing or capturing Rommel at what was thought to be his headquarters failed. On the Eastern Front, the ground had frozen and Typhoon resumed.

episode: Winter is here? The Germans can see Moscow
headline: Within sight of the Kremlin?
article: With the ground hard, Army Group Centre attacked again in mid-November in a pincer around Moscow from the north and south. Temperatures fell well below freezing and German troops without winter clothing suffered terribly from frostbite; weapons and engines froze. By late November German units in the north reached the Moscow-Volga canal and Krasnaya Polyana, about 30 kilometres from the city; some later claimed to have seen the Kremlin's spires through field glasses. In the south, Guderian bypassed Tula. Rostov was taken on 21 November and lost again on the 29th, the first major German retreat of the war. In Libya, Rommel launched a deep raid toward the Egyptian frontier.

episode: Winter is Here! The failure of Barbarossa
headline: The Soviet counteroffensive at Moscow
photo: f:RIAN archive 88775 Soviet soldiers attacking house.jpg
s:Red Army winter counteroffensive December 1941 Moscow
article: The German attack stalled in the first days of December at temperatures of minus 30 and below. On 5 December, Soviet forces north of Moscow struck back, and the next day the counteroffensive widened along the whole front. German commanders, exhausted and freezing, asked to retreat. Hitler forbade it, then dismissed generals who disobeyed. The German army had suffered its first major defeat. On 7 December, Japanese aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor and Japanese forces landed in Malaya; the United States declared war on Japan on the 8th, and Britain did the same. The war was now global.

episode: Hitler Declares War on the USA and the Jews
headline: Germany declares war on the United States
article: On 11 December Hitler told the Reichstag that Germany was at war with the United States; Italy followed the same day. He was not obliged to by the Tripartite Pact, since Japan had attacked first. He seems to have believed war with America was coming anyway and that U-boats could now be unleashed on American shipping. It was one of his most consequential decisions. On 12 December he met Nazi party leaders, and according to Goebbels's diary he spoke of the "annihilation" of the Jews as the necessary consequence of the world war he claimed they had caused. Historians see these weeks as a turning point in the decision to murder all of Europe's Jews. Mass shootings in the east were already under way; the first gassings at Chełmno began on 8 December.

episode: The Japanese are unstoppable everywhere
headline: Japan advances everywhere
photo: w:Sinking of Prince of Wales and Repulse
article: In the days after Pearl Harbor Japanese forces struck across the Pacific and South-East Asia. On 10 December Japanese aircraft sank the battleship Prince of Wales and the battlecruiser Repulse off Malaya, the first capital ships sunk at sea by aircraft alone; Churchill said he never received a more direct shock. Guam fell; Japanese troops landed in the northern Philippines; Hong Kong's mainland defences collapsed. In Malaya, Japanese troops pushed south through the jungle and on bicycles. In Russia, the Soviet counteroffensive pushed Army Group Centre back from Moscow; Kalinin was retaken on 16 December. Within a fortnight the Western position in Asia was falling apart.

episode: Heinz Guderian's Christmas and the fall of Hong Kong
headline: Hong Kong falls; Hitler takes command of the army
article: Hong Kong's British, Canadian, Indian and local defenders held the island for nearly a week against Japanese assaults before surrendering on Christmas Day, "Black Christmas". Japanese troops committed atrocities against prisoners and nurses. On 19 December Hitler dismissed the commander-in-chief of the army, Walther von Brauchitsch, and took personal command; Guderian was sacked on 26 December for retreating without permission. Hitler's order to "stand fast" did keep the German front from collapse, at a terrible cost. Churchill was in Washington for the Arcadia Conference, where the British and Americans confirmed that defeating Germany came first. The Allies had now lost every possession they held on the China coast.

episode: The Formation of the United Nations!
headline: The United Nations declaration
article: On 1 January 1942 twenty-six nations signed the "Declaration by United Nations" in Washington, pledging to use their full resources against the Axis and not to make a separate peace. The name was Roosevelt's. The Arcadia Conference created the Combined Chiefs of Staff to direct the British and American war effort, and a unified command in South-East Asia under Wavell. Manila was declared an open city and occupied on 2 January; American and Filipino troops withdrew to the Bataan peninsula. In Libya, Crusader had forced Rommel back to El Agheila, where he had started in March; Tobruk had been relieved.

episode: Washington DC Abandons The Troops in the Field
headline: Holding on at Bataan
article: About 80,000 American and Filipino troops under Douglas MacArthur dug in on the Bataan peninsula, while MacArthur himself directed the defence from the island fortress of Corregidor. They were short of food from the start, with supplies left behind in the hurried retreat, and soon on half rations. Malaria and dysentery spread. Washington knew it could not reinforce them through the Japanese blockade and decided to concentrate resources elsewhere; the men on Bataan increasingly felt abandoned. In Malaya, Japanese forces took Kuala Lumpur on 11 January. In the Soviet Union, the counteroffensive continued along the whole front. Those who were there called themselves the "battling bastards of Bataan".

episode: German U-Boats to Strike New York
headline: U-boats off the American coast
article: In mid-January five long-range U-boats arrived off the east coast of the United States in Operation Paukenschlag, Drumbeat. They found ships sailing alone with navigation lights on, coastal towns brightly lit behind them, and almost no convoy system or anti-submarine patrols. In the next months U-boats sank hundreds of ships in American waters, many of them tankers, often within sight of the shore. U-boat crews called it the "second happy time". The US Navy under Admiral King was slow to adopt convoys, partly for lack of escorts. It would take until the summer before losses were brought under control. Americans on beaches watched burning tankers at night.

episode: The Formalization of Extermination - The Wannsee Conference
headline: The Wannsee Conference
article: On 20 January fifteen senior officials of the SS, Nazi party and government ministries met at a villa on Lake Wannsee in Berlin, chaired by Reinhard Heydrich. The meeting lasted about 90 minutes. Its purpose was to coordinate the "final solution of the Jewish question" across the bureaucracy: who would be included, how mixed-ancestry cases would be treated, and how Jews from all over Europe would be deported east. The minutes, prepared by Adolf Eichmann, listed some 11 million Jews to be included. Mass murder had already begun in the occupied USSR and at Chełmno; Wannsee organised its extension to the whole continent. The villa is now a memorial and education centre. This entry is shown without map styling.

episode: Fortress Singapore Stands Alone!
headline: Singapore alone
article: On 31 January the last British and Commonwealth troops crossed the causeway from the Malayan mainland to Singapore island, and engineers blew a gap in it behind them. In under eight weeks the Japanese 25th Army under Tomoyuki Yamashita had driven the length of the Malay peninsula, outmanoeuvring larger forces with infiltration, flanking landings and bicycle-mounted infantry. Singapore had been built up for twenty years as the great naval base of the Empire in the East, but its defences were designed against attack from the sea, and there was no fleet to use it. The island was crowded with troops, refugees and civilians. In Libya, Rommel struck again on 21 January and retook Benghazi on the 29th, sending the Eighth Army back toward Gazala.

episode: Pearl Harbor Avenged!
headline: The first American carrier raids
article: On 1 February carrier task forces under William Halsey and Frank Fletcher raided Japanese bases in the Marshall and Gilbert Islands. The damage was modest, but it was the first American offensive action of the Pacific war, and it showed the carriers that had been absent from Pearl Harbor were very much in the fight. Admiral Chester Nimitz now commanded the Pacific Fleet. American newspapers called it revenge for Pearl Harbor, which overstated the case. In the Dutch East Indies, Japanese forces were moving on Sumatra, Borneo and Java, while in Burma they advanced from Thailand toward Moulmein. On the Eastern Front, Soviet attacks continued against German salients south of Leningrad and near Moscow.

episode: German Army Surrounded: You Did Nazi That Coming!
headline: Germans encircled at Demyansk
article: On 8 February Soviet forces closed a ring around about 95,000 German troops of the 16th Army at Demyansk, south of Lake Ilmen, and a smaller pocket formed at Kholm. Hitler forbade a breakout and ordered the Luftwaffe to supply the pocket by air. Transport planes flew in hundreds of tonnes a day and brought out the wounded, and the pocket held until a relief force broke through in April. The airlift worked, at a large cost in aircraft and crews, and it taught Hitler and Göring the wrong lesson about what air supply could do. Further south, Soviet forces were attempting to surround German forces near Rzhev and Vyazma, with mixed success.

episode: Britain's Worst Defeat - Singapore Falls
headline: Singapore surrenders
article: Japanese troops crossed the Johor Strait on the night of 8 February and broke through the island's defences. Water supplies were failing and the city was under constant bombardment. On 15 February Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival surrendered Singapore with about 80,000 British, Australian, Indian and local troops, the largest capitulation in British military history. Churchill called it the worst disaster in British history. Many prisoners would die building the Burma–Thailand railway. In the days after, the Japanese military police carried out the Sook Ching massacres of Chinese civilians in Singapore. On 11–13 February the German battlecruisers Scharnhorst and Gneisenau dashed up the English Channel from Brest to home waters, a humiliation for the Royal Navy and RAF.

episode: Japan Destroys Allied Armada in Biggest Naval Battle in Decades
headline: The Battle of the Java Sea
article: On 27 February a scratch force of Dutch, American, British and Australian cruisers and destroyers under the Dutch admiral Karel Doorman tried to stop a Japanese invasion convoy heading for Java. Without a common signal system or air cover, it was outfought by Japanese cruisers using long-range torpedoes. Doorman went down with his flagship De Ruyter, and over the next days most of the surviving Allied ships were sunk trying to escape, including the cruisers Houston and Perth. Darwin in northern Australia had been bombed on 19 February by the same carrier force that hit Pearl Harbor, killing over 200 people. Java was now open to invasion.

episode: The Japanese Raid Australia and the British Raid France
headline: Japan bombs Australia; Britain bombs France
article: In the first days of March, Japanese fighters raided Broome in Western Australia, destroying flying boats full of refugees from Java, and Japanese troops landed on Java itself; the Dutch surrendered on 8–9 March. In Europe, British paratroopers raided a German radar station at Bruneval on the French coast on 27–28 February and brought back key parts of a Würzburg radar. On 3–4 March RAF Bomber Command attacked the Renault works at Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris, which was building trucks for the Germans. The factory was badly damaged, but several hundred French civilians were killed. The raid foreshadowed the hard moral arithmetic of bombing occupied countries.

episode: Tumbling Capitals - MacArthur on the Run
headline: Rangoon falls; MacArthur leaves the Philippines
article: The British abandoned Rangoon on 7 March after destroying the port and oil installations; Japanese troops entered the next day. Burma's only major port was gone and with it the supply route to China by sea and the Burma Road. British, Indian and Burmese troops, with Chinese armies sent by Chiang Kai-shek, began a long fighting retreat north. On 11 March, on Roosevelt's orders, MacArthur left Corregidor by PT boat for Mindanao and then flew to Australia. On arrival he told reporters: "I shall return." The troops he left on Bataan were starving. In the Netherlands East Indies, the colonial army had surrendered.

episode: Crap Tactics in the Pacific - Shall MacArthur Return?
headline: MacArthur in Australia
article: MacArthur reached Melbourne on 21 March and was named Supreme Commander, Allied Forces, South West Pacific Area. The Pacific was split into two commands: MacArthur's to the south-west and Nimitz's Pacific Ocean Areas, a division driven by inter-service rivalry that would shape the whole war. Australia's prime minister John Curtin had already announced that his country now looked to America rather than Britain for its defence, and Australian divisions were brought home from the Middle East. Japanese forces took the Andaman Islands and pushed into New Guinea. In Burma, the Allied retreat continued, and in the Philippines, American and Filipino troops on Bataan were down to quarter rations.

episode: New Blitzkrieg Against a Wall of 9 Million!
headline: The Red Army after its first winter
article: The Soviet winter counteroffensive had saved Moscow but then overreached. Stalin had ordered attacks along the whole front instead of concentrating, and by March they had largely stalled in the thaw. In the north, the Second Shock Army had pushed into a narrow salient toward Lyuban in an attempt to relieve Leningrad and was now in danger of being cut off. Both armies were rebuilding: the Red Army had nine million men under arms by the spring, but much of it was poorly trained. On 28 March Hitler issued instructions for the summer offensive in the south, aimed at the Caucasus oil fields. Soviet commanders expected the main German blow to fall on Moscow again.

episode: The Carpet Bombing of Germany begins
headline: Bomber Command burns Lübeck
photo: w:Bombing of Lübeck in World War II
article: On the night of 28–29 March RAF Bomber Command dropped large numbers of incendiaries on the medieval Hanseatic city of Lübeck, whose narrow streets and timber buildings burned easily. Much of the old town was destroyed and over 300 people were killed. It was the first major success for the new head of Bomber Command, Arthur Harris, who had taken over in February with a directive to target the morale of German civilians, in practice the centres of cities. Hitler ordered retaliatory "Baedeker raids" on historic English towns, including Exeter, Bath, Norwich and York. On 28 March British commandos rammed an explosive-filled destroyer into the dock gates at St Nazaire, wrecking the only Atlantic dock able to hold the battleship Tirpitz.

episode: America Surrenders - The Fall of Bataan
headline: Bataan surrenders
article: On 9 April Major General Edward King surrendered about 75,000 American and Filipino troops on Bataan, starving, sick and out of ammunition. It was the largest surrender of US forces in history. Japanese forces then marched the prisoners about 100 kilometres to a railhead in tropical heat with little food or water; those who fell behind were often beaten, bayoneted or shot. Thousands of Filipinos and hundreds of Americans died on what became known as the Bataan Death March, and many more died in the camps afterwards. Corregidor held out for another month. Japanese carriers raided Ceylon in early April and sank the British carrier Hermes and two cruisers.

episode: America Strikes Back - Tokyo in Flames
headline: The Doolittle raid on Tokyo
article: On 18 April sixteen US Army B-25 bombers, led by Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle, took off from the carrier Hornet about 1,000 kilometres from Japan and bombed Tokyo, Yokohama, Nagoya and Kobe. The damage was slight; most aircraft ran out of fuel and crash-landed in China, where Chinese civilians helped the crews escape. Japan took brutal reprisals against Chinese villages suspected of helping. The raid gave a huge boost to American morale, and it rattled Japan's leaders, who had promised the home islands were untouchable. It strengthened Admiral Yamamoto's case for an operation to destroy the US carriers at Midway.

episode: Allied Intelligence cracks Japanese codes!
headline: Codebreakers read the Japanese plans
article: At Pearl Harbor, the US Navy codebreaking unit known as Station HYPO, led by Commander Joseph Rochefort, had been working on the main Japanese naval code, JN-25. By late April it could read enough of the traffic to detect that Japan was preparing an operation against Port Moresby in New Guinea, to be covered by aircraft carriers. Nimitz acted on the intelligence and sent his own carriers south to the Coral Sea. The codebreakers also picked up hints of a larger operation in the central Pacific. In Burma, the Japanese captured Lashio on 29 April, cutting the Burma Road to China. In Germany, Hitler addressed the Reichstag on 26 April and was granted unlimited legal powers.

episode: Japan - One Battle from Victory?
headline: Japan at the height of its power
article: By the end of April Japan controlled an empire stretching from Burma to the Gilbert Islands and from the Aleutians to the borders of Australia. It had done so in under five months at modest cost. Mandalay fell on 1 May. General Joseph Stilwell, the American commander of Chinese troops in Burma, walked out to India with a small party and told reporters, "We got a hell of a beating." Japan's naval leaders debated where to strike next: Australia, Hawaii, India or the Aleutians. Some believed one more decisive victory would force the Americans to negotiate. Few in Tokyo had a plan for how the war would actually end.

episode: Carrier vs. Carrier - The Battle of Coral Sea
headline: Carrier against carrier in the Coral Sea
article: From 4 to 8 May American and Japanese carrier forces fought the Battle of the Coral Sea, the first naval battle in which the opposing ships never saw each other: all the fighting was done by aircraft. The US lost the carrier Lexington and Japan the light carrier Shoho; the Japanese carrier Shokaku was badly damaged and Zuikaku lost many aircraft. Tactically it was close to a draw, but the Japanese called off their seaborne invasion of Port Moresby, their first strategic check of the war. Neither of the two big Japanese carriers would be available for Midway. Corregidor surrendered on 6 May.

episode: Joseph Stalin Jumps the Gun
headline: Stalin's offensive at Kharkov fails
article: On 12 May the Red Army under Timoshenko attacked from the Izium bulge to retake Kharkov, Ukraine's second city. Stalin had insisted on offensives despite advice to stay on the defensive until the Germans showed their hand. The southern pincer pushed forward, but on 17 May German forces struck the base of the bulge. Requests to call off the attack were refused until too late. By the end of the month several Soviet armies had been surrounded and over 200,000 men captured. In Crimea, German and Romanian forces under Manstein had destroyed Soviet forces on the Kerch peninsula. The road was open for the German summer offensive.

episode: AF is short of fresh water
headline: "AF is short of water"
article: American codebreakers knew a major Japanese operation was coming against a target designated "AF", but Washington doubted it was Midway. Rochefort's team had the garrison on Midway send an uncoded radio message reporting that its water distillation plant had broken down. Within days a Japanese intercept reported that "AF" was short of water. Nimitz now knew where and roughly when. He ordered the damaged carrier Yorktown repaired in three days instead of the estimated three months, and positioned his three carriers north-east of Midway to ambush the Japanese fleet. In Czechoslovakia, Czech and Slovak parachutists from Britain attacked Reinhard Heydrich in Prague on 27 May.

episode: Rommel's Desert Dash - The Whole Bloody Afrika Korps! - Gazala
headline: Rommel attacks at Gazala
article: On 26 May Rommel attacked the Eighth Army's Gazala line, a string of fortified "boxes" protected by minefields running south from the coast west of Tobruk. He swung his armour around the southern end at Bir Hakeim, where a Free French brigade under General Koenig held out for two weeks. The battle that followed was confused and bloody. Rommel's forces, briefly trapped in an area the British called "the Cauldron", broke out and destroyed British armour that attacked piecemeal. On the night of 30–31 May, Bomber Command sent over 1,000 bombers against Cologne for the first time, a show of strength that killed 469 people and made headlines worldwide.

episode: Midway, pt.1 - Clash of the Titans
headline: Midway: four carriers in five minutes
photo: f:SBD-3 Dauntless bombers of VS-8 over the burning Japanese cruiser Mikuma on 6 June 1942.jpg
article: On the morning of 4 June Japanese aircraft attacked Midway while American carriers launched their strikes. Torpedo planes attacked first and were cut to pieces. But their attacks drew the Japanese fighters down, and around 10:20 dive-bombers from the Enterprise and Yorktown found three Japanese carriers, Akagi, Kaga and Soryu, with aircraft refuelling and rearming on their decks. Within minutes all three were burning wrecks. The fourth, Hiryu, launched strikes that crippled Yorktown before being sunk herself that afternoon. Japan lost four fleet carriers and many experienced aircrew. It was the turning point of the Pacific war. In five minutes the balance of the Pacific war had changed.

episode: Germany to Strike Strongest Fortress in the World
headline: Manstein moves on Sevastopol
article: In early June Manstein's 11th Army prepared its final assault on Sevastopol, the Soviet naval base in Crimea, besieged since November 1941. It was one of the strongest fortified positions in the world, with heavy forts, coastal batteries and tunnels. The Germans assembled an enormous artillery park, including the giant railway gun "Dora" with 80cm shells and huge mortars, and began a five-day bombardment on 2 June. The Luftwaffe flew hundreds of sorties a day. The defenders, about 100,000 soldiers and marines, had little hope of rescue. Capturing the port would free Manstein's army for the summer offensive and remove a Soviet base on the Black Sea.

episode: Midway pt.2 - A New War?
headline: After Midway: a different war
article: The battle ended on 6–7 June. American dive-bombers sank the heavy cruiser Mikuma; a Japanese submarine finished off the Yorktown and a destroyer alongside her. Japan had lost four carriers and a cruiser; America one carrier and a destroyer. More important than the ships were the trained crews and pilots, which Japan could not replace quickly, while American shipyards were building carriers at a rate Japan could not match. The Japanese government concealed the scale of the defeat from its own people. On 7 June Japanese forces occupied Attu and Kiska in the Aleutians, a diversion that won barren islands. The Pacific war now turned toward attrition, and the Americans began planning their first offensive.

episode: Sevastopol Must Fall!
headline: The storming of Sevastopol
article: After the bombardment, German and Romanian infantry attacked Sevastopol's northern and eastern defences on 7 June. The fighting for the forts, tunnels and ridges was savage and slow, and German casualties mounted fast. The defenders, short of ammunition and cut off from supply by sea as the Luftwaffe sank the ships trying to reach them, were gradually pushed back toward the city and the Chersonese peninsula. In Prague, Heydrich had died of his wounds on 4 June. On 10 June, in reprisal, German forces destroyed the village of Lidice, shooting its 173 men and sending its women and children to camps, where most of the children were murdered. The regime announced it publicly as a warning.

episode: Tobruk: A second siege?
headline: Tobruk under threat again
article: At Gazala, Rommel's forces broke the British line in the second week of June. Bir Hakeim was evacuated by the Free French on 10–11 June after a defence that made Koenig's name. On 12–13 June, in the battles around "Knightsbridge", British armour suffered heavy losses, and the Eighth Army began a disorderly retreat toward the Egyptian frontier, leaving the garrison of Tobruk, mostly South African troops, to hold the port. Unlike in 1941, its defences had been neglected and its garrison was not prepared for a siege. In the Mediterranean, two convoys trying to relieve Malta from east and west in mid-June were mauled; only two merchant ships got through.

episode: Fall Blau Starts...or Does it?
headline: Tobruk falls in a day
article: On 20 June Rommel attacked Tobruk from the south-east after a heavy air and artillery bombardment. The defences cracked within hours, and on 21 June the South African commander, General Klopper, surrendered with about 33,000 men and large stocks of fuel and supplies. Rommel was promoted to field marshal. Churchill heard the news in the White House while meeting Roosevelt; he later called it one of the heaviest blows of the war. Roosevelt asked what America could do, and offered Sherman tanks to the Eighth Army. In Russia, the German summer offensive was poised to start; on 19 June a plane carrying German plans for it crashed behind Soviet lines.

episode: Fall Blau Begins, Stalin Caught off Guard Again
headline: Fall Blau begins
article: On 28 June German forces launched Fall Blau, Case Blue, the summer offensive in southern Russia. Army Group South attacked east toward Voronezh on the Don, and then swung south-east along the river. Its aims were to destroy the Soviet armies in the bend of the Don, reach the Volga near Stalingrad, and then drive into the Caucasus to seize the oil fields. Stalin, despite the captured plans, still believed the main danger was to Moscow. Soviet resistance was spotty and German armour advanced fast across the open steppe. Sevastopol fell on 4 July after a month of siege. In Egypt, the Eighth Army stopped Rommel at the first battle of El Alamein, starting 1 July.

episode: Fall Blau - A Victim of Its Own Success?
headline: Rommel stopped at El Alamein
article: El Alamein was a railway halt about 100 kilometres west of Alexandria, where the desert narrowed between the sea and the impassable Qattara Depression to a gap of 60 kilometres. Auchinleck, who had taken direct command of the Eighth Army, stopped Rommel's exhausted forces there in the first days of July and counterattacked repeatedly through the month. In Cairo, the British embassy had burned papers in what became known as "Ash Wednesday". On the Eastern Front, German troops took Voronezh. In the Arctic, convoy PQ 17 was ordered to scatter on 4 July after a false alarm that the Tirpitz was out; U-boats and aircraft sank 24 of its 35 merchant ships.

episode: Stalingrad Now a Primary Objective?! - Hitler's Chaotic Directives
headline: Hitler splits the offensive
article: On 13 July Hitler sacked Field Marshal von Bock, commander of Army Group South, for delays at Voronezh. He split the army group in two: Army Group A would drive south into the Caucasus, and Army Group B would advance to the Volga at Stalingrad. On 23 July his Directive 45 ordered both to proceed at once rather than one after the other, overstretching forces that were already short of fuel. In the field, the Germans were advancing fast but taking far fewer prisoners than in 1941, because Soviet commanders were now allowed to retreat and did. Some German generals read this as a sign of collapse; others saw a trap.

episode: Wehrmacht Conquers 250 Miles of Nothing
headline: Across empty steppe to the Don
article: German armour drove south-east across the steppe of the Don bend in July, covering huge distances against little resistance. Rostov, the gateway to the Caucasus, fell on 23–24 July after a short battle. The Wehrmacht had gained territory but not destroyed the Soviet armies it had come to encircle; they had retreated across the Don. German supply lines were stretched; fuel ran out frequently. In occupied Europe, the deportation of Jews was accelerating: the Vel' d'Hiv round-up in Paris on 16–17 July seized more than 13,000 Jews, including over 4,000 children, arrested by French police. The great deportations from the Warsaw Ghetto to Treblinka began on 22 July.

episode: How Hitler Created the World's Worst Traffic Jam
headline: The great traffic jam on the Don
article: In late July Hitler ordered most of the panzer forces of both army groups to converge on the lower Don near Rostov to trap Soviet armies thought to be there. The armies were not there, and the result was a massive traffic jam of armour, trucks and supply columns on a few river crossings, while the drive on Stalingrad was starved of fuel and the Sixth Army advanced with infantry alone. The Fourth Panzer Army was then turned back toward Stalingrad from the south, wasting more time and fuel. Hitler's interference created confusion at exactly the moment when speed mattered most. Soviet forces used the lull to fortify the approaches to Stalingrad.

episode: Not a Step Back! - Wehrmacht Closes in on Stalingrad
headline: "Not a step back!"
article: On 28 July Stalin issued Order No. 227, read out to every unit: "Not a step back!" It acknowledged that the Soviet Union had lost huge territory and that further retreat would mean ruin. Officers and commissars who allowed unauthorised withdrawal would be court-martialled; blocking detachments were authorised to stop soldiers fleeing; penal battalions were created. The order came after Rostov's fall and a period of panic in the south. German forces of the Sixth Army under Friedrich Paulus reached the big bend of the Don west of Stalingrad. In the Caucasus, Army Group A pushed toward Maikop and the oil fields.

episode: Guadalcanal - Allies Take the Initiative
headline: The Marines land on Guadalcanal
article: On 7 August about 11,000 US Marines landed on Guadalcanal and neighbouring islands in the Solomons, where the Japanese were building an airfield that could threaten the supply route between the US and Australia. It was the first American land offensive of the war. The landings met little resistance and the airfield, renamed Henderson Field, was taken the next day. But on the night of 8–9 August a Japanese cruiser force surprised the Allied naval screen off Savo Island and sank four heavy cruisers. The transports withdrew, leaving the Marines short of supplies. Both sides began pouring men, aircraft and ships into a campaign that would last six months.

episode: No Soviet Oil for Hitler
headline: The oil fields burn
article: German armour of Army Group A reached Maikop, the first of the Caucasus oil centres, on 9 August, only to find the oil wells and refineries wrecked by retreating Soviet engineers. It would take months to produce any oil at all, and the much larger fields at Grozny and Baku were still far away over mountains. The advance slowed as fuel shortages bit and Soviet resistance stiffened along the passes. On 12 August Churchill arrived in Moscow to tell Stalin there would be no second front in Europe in 1942, only an invasion of North Africa. The meeting was tense, though the two men ended it drinking until the early morning.

episode: Swastika Raised on Highest Point in Europe
headline: The swastika on Elbrus
article: On 21 August German mountain troops climbed Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in the Caucasus and in Europe, and planted the Reich war flag on its summit. Propaganda made much of it; Hitler was furious that his troops were climbing mountains while the oil fields remained out of reach. On 19 August, a mostly Canadian force raided the French port of Dieppe. Of about 6,000 men, nearly 1,000 were killed and around 2,000 captured in a few hours. The raid was a costly lesson in how not to attack a defended port. On 23 August, German forces reached the Volga north of Stalingrad, and the Luftwaffe bombed the city heavily.

episode: Yamamoto: Midway Round Two?
headline: The carriers clash again
article: On 24–25 August American and Japanese carrier forces fought the Battle of the Eastern Solomons as Japan tried to land reinforcements on Guadalcanal. The Japanese lost the light carrier Ryujo and many aircraft; the Enterprise was damaged. The Japanese convoy turned back, and from then on Japan increasingly moved troops to Guadalcanal at night by fast destroyers, which the Americans called the "Tokyo Express". On the island, Marines had repulsed a Japanese attack at the Tenaru River on 21 August, almost wiping out the assault force. In New Guinea, Japanese troops pushing over the Kokoda Track toward Port Moresby and landing at Milne Bay met determined Australian resistance.

episode: This War is Three Years Old
headline: Three years of war
article: The war entered its fourth year with the Axis at its greatest extent: Germans on the Volga and in the Caucasus, Rommel 100 kilometres from Alexandria, Japan holding an empire across Asia and the Pacific. At El Alamein, Rommel's last attempt to break through at Alam Halfa between 30 August and 5 September was stopped by the Eighth Army's new commander, Bernard Montgomery. At Stalingrad, the German Sixth Army and Fourth Panzer Army closed on the city from the west and south. Soviet troops of the 62nd Army were pushed back into the city itself. At sea, U-boat sinkings were reaching their peak.

episode: Hitler Finally Fed Up with his Army
headline: Hitler turns on his generals
article: From his forward headquarters at Vinnytsia in Ukraine, Hitler raged at the slow progress in the Caucasus and the Don. On 9 September he dismissed Field Marshal List and took personal command of Army Group A himself, from hundreds of kilometres away. On 24 September he dismissed the army chief of staff Franz Halder, who had argued with him over Stalingrad and the overstretched front, replacing him with Kurt Zeitzler. Hitler refused to shake hands with Jodl for months after a disagreement and had stenographers record every word of his military conferences from then on. The German high command was becoming a place where telling the truth was risky.

episode: Stalingrad, Hitler's Obsession
headline: Stalingrad becomes an obsession
article: By mid-September the battle for Stalingrad itself had begun. The city's symbolic name was now more important to both dictators than its military value, which mainly lay in blocking the Volga as a supply route. Paulus's Sixth Army attacked the city centre on 13 September. Soviet General Vasily Chuikov, who had taken command of the 62nd Army the day before, kept his units close to the Germans so that their artillery and aircraft could not strike without hitting their own men. The Soviet 13th Guards Division crossed the Volga under fire on the night of 14–15 September and retook the central station and the Mamayev Kurgan hill.

episode: Stalingrad Falls?
headline: Stalingrad does not fall
article: Through mid-September German troops fought block by block into central Stalingrad, taking the main railway station, which changed hands many times, and reaching the Volga in the city centre. German news agencies prematurely reported that the city had fallen. Soviet reinforcements crossed the river nightly in boats under fire, many of them killed before they reached the bank. The giant grain elevator in the south of the city was defended for days by a small group of Soviet troops. In Moscow, Zhukov and Vasilevsky proposed to Stalin a counteroffensive, later code-named Uranus, against the weak Romanian armies on the flanks.

episode: Stalingrad, Factory by Factory, Room by Room
headline: Factory by factory, room by room
article: By late September the battle had moved to the great factory district in the north of Stalingrad: the Tractor Factory, the Barrikady gun works and the Red October steel plant. Fighting went on in workshops, cellars and sewers, often at a few metres' range. German troops called it Rattenkrieg, rat war. Soviet snipers became heroes in the press. Losses on both sides were enormous; a Soviet rifleman sent across the Volga might survive only days. Chuikov's army held only narrow strips along the river bank, but it held. The Soviet command fed in just enough men to keep the defence alive while it quietly gathered armies north and south of the city for the counter-stroke.

episode: This is Russia, The Soviet Thermopylae
headline: The Soviet Thermopylae
article: Soviet propaganda compared the defence of Stalingrad to the stand at Thermopylae. The hill of Mamayev Kurgan, which overlooked the city and the river crossings, changed hands repeatedly; its soil was later found to contain huge quantities of shell fragments. A building in the city centre held for nearly two months by a small group under Sergeant Yakov Pavlov became known as Pavlov's House. In the Caucasus the German advance had stalled short of Grozny and in the mountains above the Black Sea coast. In Egypt, Montgomery was building up the Eighth Army for a set-piece offensive, with new Sherman tanks arriving from America.

episode: Stalingrad Thunderdome: Paulus vs. Chuikov!
headline: Paulus against Chuikov
article: Friedrich Paulus, a careful staff officer commanding the Sixth Army, launched a series of attacks in October to clear the remaining Soviet bridgeheads on the Volga. On 14 October a massive assault on the Tractor Factory pushed the Germans to the river in the north and nearly split the 62nd Army. Vasily Chuikov, tough, blunt and willing to accept enormous losses, moved his headquarters into a bunker close to the river bank and kept counterattacking. German infantry companies were down to a few dozen men. Hitler declared in a speech that Stalingrad would be taken and that no power on earth would remove the Germans from it.

episode: Stalingrad, Stalingrad, Stalingrad, No Retreat!
headline: No retreat at Stalingrad
article: Mid-October saw some of the fiercest fighting of the battle. German troops took the Tractor Factory and pushed to the Volga at several points; the Barrikady works became the next target. Soviet artillery on the east bank of the river, firing across the water, helped make each German gain enormously expensive. The Luftwaffe kept the city under constant attack. Chuikov's units were sometimes reduced to a few hundred metres from the water's edge. On the Soviet side of the river, preparations for Operation Uranus were advanced: over a million men, thousands of tanks and guns, moved in secret at night. The planned date was early November, later moved to 19 November.

episode: Showdown at El Alamein
headline: Showdown at El Alamein
article: On the night of 23 October, more than 800 British guns opened fire along the El Alamein line, starting the second battle of El Alamein. Montgomery's Eighth Army had about 195,000 men and over 1,000 tanks against roughly 116,000 German and Italian troops with about 550 tanks. Engineers cleared paths through the deep Axis minefields, which Rommel called the "Devil's gardens", for the armour to pass. Rommel himself was in Germany on sick leave when the attack began. The first days brought little progress at a heavy cost. Montgomery called it a "dogfight" and kept up the pressure, shifting his attacks to wear down the Axis forces.

episode: Nazi General Dies of Heart Attack
headline: A general dies; Rommel returns
article: On the first day of El Alamein, General Georg Stumme, commanding in Rommel's absence, drove to the front and came under fire; he died of a heart attack. Rommel flew back on 25 October to find his armour being worn down and his fuel reserves almost gone; British submarines and aircraft had sunk several tankers bound for North Africa. He counterattacked repeatedly against the British salients and lost tanks he could not replace. Australian troops attacked toward the coast in the north, drawing in German reserves. In the Solomons, the Battle of Santa Cruz on 26 October cost the US the carrier Hornet; Japan lost many experienced aircrew.

episode: The Allies Break Through!
headline: The breakthrough at El Alamein
article: On 2 November Montgomery launched Operation Supercharge, a new thrust by British and New Zealand forces. After heavy fighting the Axis front cracked. On 3 November Hitler ordered Rommel to stand fast, "victory or death". Rommel obeyed for a day, then retreated on 4 November with what was left of his armour, leaving behind many of the Italian infantry, who had no transport. About 30,000 Axis soldiers were captured. Churchill ordered church bells rung across Britain on 15 November, the first time since 1940. He later wrote that before Alamein the Allies never had a victory, and after it they never had a defeat, which was not true but became famous.

episode: Axis and Allies Both Invade France
headline: Operation Torch; Germany occupies Vichy France
article: On 8 November British and American forces landed in French North Africa at Casablanca, Oran and Algiers. Vichy French forces resisted for several days, at a cost of over a thousand dead on each side. Admiral François Darlan, Pétain's deputy, happened to be in Algiers, and the Americans did a deal with him to order a ceasefire on 10 November, to the outrage of the Free French and many Allied supporters. Hitler responded on 11 November by sending troops into the unoccupied zone of France, ending Vichy's nominal independence. Germany also rushed troops into Tunisia by air. On 27 November the French fleet at Toulon scuttled itself rather than fall to the Germans.

episode: The Red Army Kicks Ass - Operation Uranus!
headline: Operation Uranus
article: At 7:20 on the morning of 19 November, Soviet artillery opened fire on the Romanian Third Army north-west of Stalingrad. The next day a second attack struck the Romanian Fourth Army to the south. The Romanian troops were poorly equipped and short of anti-tank guns; they fought bravely in places but their lines collapsed. Soviet tank corps drove deep behind the German Sixth Army. In Libya, the Eighth Army retook Tobruk on 13 November and Benghazi on 20 November. On Guadalcanal, the decisive naval battle of 12–15 November ended Japan's main effort to reinforce the island. Within three days the two Romanian armies had ceased to exist as fighting forces.

episode: Bigger Than Uranus? - Mars
headline: The Sixth Army is trapped; Operation Mars fails
article: On 23 November Soviet tank spearheads from north and south met at Kalach on the Don, encircling about 300,000 German and Axis troops in and around Stalingrad. Paulus asked for freedom to break out. Göring promised that the Luftwaffe could supply the pocket by air, which was never realistic, and Hitler ordered the Sixth Army to hold "Fortress Stalingrad". At the same time, a massive Soviet offensive, Operation Mars, under Zhukov, was launched against the German salient at Rzhev, west of Moscow. It failed with enormous losses and was barely mentioned in Soviet histories for decades. Uranus succeeded; Mars did not.

episode: Axis Armies Facing Starvation
headline: The airlift fails
article: The Sixth Army needed at least 300 tonnes of supplies a day by air; the Luftwaffe rarely delivered a third of that. Transport aircraft were shot down by Soviet fighters and anti-aircraft guns, grounded by winter weather, or lost on the airfields that the Soviets kept pushing back. Inside the pocket, rations were cut, horses were slaughtered, and fuel ran out. Field Marshal Manstein was put in charge of a new Army Group Don to relieve Stalingrad. In Tunisia, German forces stopped the Allied drive on Tunis in early December. In North Africa, Darlan was assassinated in Algiers on 24 December.

episode: One Year Since Pearl Harbor
headline: A year since Pearl Harbor
photo: s:USS Arizona memorial Pearl Harbor 1942 salvage
article: On 7 December the United States marked the first anniversary of Pearl Harbor. In a year, the country had built a war economy of enormous scale: production of aircraft, tanks and ships was multiplying, and over five million men were in uniform. American forces had fought Japan to a standstill at Midway and on Guadalcanal and were in North Africa. On 2 December, in a squash court under the stands of a Chicago stadium, scientists led by Enrico Fermi had produced the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. On 12 December Manstein's relief offensive, Operation Winter Storm, set out from the south-west toward Stalingrad.

episode: Guadalcanal Life Expectancy: 30 Days
headline: Guadalcanal's war of attrition
article: By December the Marines who had landed in August were exhausted, many sick with malaria and other tropical diseases; they began to be relieved by Army units. Japanese troops on the island, cut off from regular supply, were starving. Japanese soldiers called it "Starvation Island". The night supply runs of the Tokyo Express could not keep pace. In Tokyo, the high command debated whether to abandon it. Manstein's relief force fought within about 50 kilometres of the Stalingrad pocket, but on 16 December the Soviets launched Operation Little Saturn against the Italian Eighth Army further north, threatening Manstein's rear. Nobody on either side expected the island to be easy.

episode: A Red Christmas
headline: A red Christmas
article: Little Saturn shattered the Italian Eighth Army on the middle Don and sent Soviet tanks deep into the German rear, including a raid on the airfield at Tatsinskaya that destroyed dozens of transport aircraft on 24 December. Manstein had to call off Winter Storm on 23 December and pull back; Paulus had never been given permission to break out to meet him. The Sixth Army spent Christmas in the pocket in freezing cold, on starvation rations. Soviet loudspeakers broadcast the ticking of a clock and the message that a German soldier died every seven seconds in Russia. The Italian retreat across the frozen steppe in the following weeks was a disaster.

episode: And Now It's 1943...
headline: The year turns at Stalingrad
article: As 1943 began, the Germans in Stalingrad were beyond rescue. In the Caucasus, Army Group A began to withdraw on 1 January to avoid being cut off by the Soviet advance toward Rostov. At the Casablanca Conference later in January, Roosevelt and Churchill would agree to demand the unconditional surrender of the Axis powers. In the Pacific, Japanese forces at Buna in New Guinea were overwhelmed by Australian and American troops on 2 January after weeks of bitter fighting. In Germany, Goebbels prepared the population for bad news. The Allies were now attacking everywhere, and the initiative had passed from the Axis.

episode: A Soviet Offensive Along the Entire Front?
headline: The Red Army attacks along the front
article: Early January brought Soviet attacks along much of the southern front. Soviet forces pressed toward Rostov from the north-east, trying to cut off Army Group A as it pulled back from the Caucasus. In the Stalingrad pocket, Soviet commanders offered Paulus surrender terms on 8 January. Under orders from Hitler, he refused. On 10 January Operation Koltso, Ring, began with a massive bombardment; the pocket was pushed back and its last airfields were lost. German troops inside were starving and freezing; many were wounded or sick with no hope of evacuation. Hitler kept promoting the trapped officers in the hope they would fight on.

episode: Food for Leningrad, Breaking the Siege!
headline: A corridor into Leningrad
article: On 12 January Soviet troops from inside Leningrad and from the Volkhov front attacked from both sides of the German-held corridor south of Lake Ladoga, in Operation Iskra, Spark. On 18 January they met, opening a land corridor about ten kilometres wide along the lake shore. A railway was built across it in under three weeks, under German artillery fire. The siege was not lifted, but food and supplies could now reach the city by rail. Some 800,000 civilians had died in Leningrad by this point, most from starvation in the winter of 1941–42. The road across the frozen lake, the "Road of Life", had kept the city alive until now.

episode: Hitler's Interference is losing the war
headline: Hitler's interference and its price
article: By mid-January the Stalingrad pocket had shrunk dramatically and its main airfield at Pitomnik was lost on 16 January. The last flights out from Gumrak carried the wounded and the mail. Further north, Soviet forces smashed the Hungarian Second Army on the Don near Voronezh in an offensive that began on 13 January; the Hungarians lost around 100,000 men. Hitler insisted every position be held, even where withdrawal could have saved armies, and his generals increasingly saw his decisions as the main cause of the disaster. At Casablanca, Churchill and Roosevelt met from 14 to 24 January and announced the unconditional surrender demand.

episode: Time to Fire Rommel?
headline: Tripoli falls; Rommel's future in doubt
article: On 23 January the Eighth Army entered Tripoli, the capital of Italian Libya, three months after Alamein and some 2,200 kilometres further west. Mussolini's African empire was gone. Rommel, tired and ill, withdrew to the Mareth Line, old French fortifications in southern Tunisia. Italian and German commanders were frustrated with him; the Italian high command wanted him replaced. In Tunisia, Axis forces under General Hans-Jürgen von Arnim held a bridgehead around Tunis and Bizerte. On the Eastern Front, the Stalingrad pocket was split in two on 26 January. Paulus remained in a department store basement in the city centre. The desert war was entering its last act.

episode: Stalingrad: Endgame
headline: Stalingrad: the end
article: On 30 January Hitler promoted Paulus to field marshal, a hint that no German field marshal had ever surrendered and that he should kill himself. Paulus surrendered the next day, 31 January, in the basement of the Univermag department store. The northern pocket gave up on 2 February. About 91,000 German and Axis soldiers went into captivity, including 22 generals; only some 5,000 would return home, the last in 1955. Germany declared three days of national mourning. Soviet losses in the battle were over a million killed, wounded and captured. Stalingrad did not end the war, but it ended the belief, in Germany and outside it, that Germany could win it.

episode: Guadalcanal, A New Offensive
headline: The last offensive on Guadalcanal
article: In January the American XIV Corps under General Alexander Patch, now including Army and Marine divisions, launched an offensive to clear the remaining Japanese from Guadalcanal. Japanese forces, starving and diseased, fought delaying actions in the hills west of Henderson Field. What the Americans did not know was that Tokyo had already decided on 31 December to withdraw. Between 1 and 7 February, fast destroyers evacuated some 10,000 Japanese troops at night in Operation Ke, an operation the Americans mistook for another reinforcement. On the Eastern Front, Soviet forces were pushing west toward Kursk and Kharkov, and on 8 February they retook Kursk.

episode: Victory at Guadalcanal
headline: Victory on Guadalcanal
article: On 9 February Patch reported that organised Japanese resistance on Guadalcanal had ended: "Tokyo Express no longer has terminus on Guadalcanal." The six-month campaign had cost Japan around 25,000 dead, many from starvation and disease, along with hundreds of aircraft and dozens of warships. American losses were about 7,000 dead. Combined with Midway, it ended Japan's ability to expand and began a war of attrition Japan could not win. In Tunisia, German forces under Rommel prepared a counteroffensive against the inexperienced US II Corps. On the Eastern Front, the Red Army retook Rostov on 14 February. Neither side would forget the lessons of the campaign.

episode: Can the Red Army Capture Hitler?
headline: Kharkov liberated, briefly
article: On 16 February Soviet troops entered Kharkov, which German forces had abandoned against Hitler's orders. Soviet armies pushed south-west toward the Dnieper, and it looked to Moscow as though the German southern front was collapsing. Hitler flew to Manstein's headquarters at Zaporizhzhia on 17 February, while Soviet tanks were just kilometres away. Manstein persuaded him to allow a mobile defence and a counterstroke. On 18 February, in Berlin, Goebbels gave his "Total War" speech at the Sportpalast to a hand-picked audience. In Munich, the Gestapo arrested Hans and Sophie Scholl of the White Rose resistance group, who were executed four days later.

episode: The Blitzkrieg is Back
headline: Kasserine: the Americans learn hard
article: On 14 February German armour struck the US II Corps at Sidi Bou Zid in central Tunisia, then pushed through the Kasserine Pass on 19–20 February. Inexperienced American units, poorly led and spread thin, were badly beaten and lost hundreds of tanks and vehicles. The Axis advance was finally stopped by American artillery and British reinforcements. The US Army learned fast: Eisenhower replaced the II Corps commander, Lloyd Fredendall, with George Patton. On the Eastern Front, Manstein's counteroffensive began on 19–20 February against the overextended Soviet forces south of Kharkov, catching their spearheads short of fuel and supplies. It was a painful but short apprenticeship.

episode: Another Naval Disaster for Japan
headline: Disaster for Japan in the Bismarck Sea
article: Between 2 and 4 March US and Australian aircraft caught a Japanese convoy carrying troops from Rabaul to Lae in New Guinea. Using new low-level "skip bombing" techniques, they sank all eight transports and four of the eight escorting destroyers. Thousands of Japanese soldiers drowned. Japan would no longer risk large convoys within range of Allied aircraft in New Guinea. Allied airmen also strafed survivors in the water and in lifeboats, an episode that reflected the brutality of the Pacific war. In Tunisia, Rommel's attack on the British at Medenine on 6 March was beaten off with heavy losses, his last battle in Africa.

episode: Rommel Leaves Africa
headline: Rommel leaves Africa
article: After the failure at Medenine, Rommel left Africa on 9 March, ostensibly on sick leave, and never returned. He urged Hitler to evacuate the army from Tunisia; Hitler refused. Von Arnim took command of all Axis forces in Africa. The Allies were closing in from west and south. On the Eastern Front, Manstein's counteroffensive pressed toward Kharkov, with SS panzer divisions leading the attack. At sea, the Battle of the Atlantic was approaching its crisis: in the first weeks of March, U-boat wolf packs sank dozens of ships from convoys SC 121, HX 228, HX 229 and SC 122, the worst losses of the war.

episode: Kharkov Falls Once Again
headline: Kharkov falls again
article: On 14–15 March the II SS Panzer Corps retook Kharkov after days of street fighting, and on 18 March German forces took Belgorod. Manstein's counteroffensive had stabilised the southern front and destroyed several Soviet formations, but the spring thaw now turned the roads to mud and stopped operations. The front settled with a large bulge projecting west around the city of Kursk, held by the Red Army, which both sides would soon target. In the North Atlantic, convoy losses peaked. Admiralty planners briefly feared the convoy system itself might fail. More escort carriers and long-range aircraft were being sent to close the mid-Atlantic air gap.

episode: American Army Finally Does Something Right
headline: Patton's corps fights well
article: On 23 March, at El Guettar in southern Tunisia, the US 1st Infantry Division beat off an attack by the German 10th Panzer Division, destroying dozens of tanks with artillery and anti-tank guns. Coming a month after Kasserine, it was the first clear American success against German armour. Patton was learning how to use his corps, and the US Army was learning how to fight. To the south-east, Montgomery's Eighth Army attacked the Mareth Line from 20 March, and when a frontal assault stalled, sent the New Zealand Corps on a wide outflanking march through the Tebaga Gap that forced the Axis forces to withdraw.

episode: The End of Hydra?
headline: The Partisans survive the Axis offensive
article: In the mountains of Bosnia, Croatia and Montenegro, Josip Broz Tito's communist-led Partisans had built an army of tens of thousands. In early 1943 German, Italian and Croatian forces launched a major offensive, Case White, to destroy them. The Partisans retreated across the Neretva river in March, carrying thousands of wounded; their escape became central to postwar Yugoslav legend. During the fighting, Partisan envoys secretly negotiated with German officers over prisoner exchanges and a possible truce, while also fighting the royalist Chetniks of Draža Mihailović. Britain was beginning to reconsider which Yugoslav resistance movement to back. In time, London switched its support from Mihailović to Tito.

episode: Patton Has a Plan, and it's Bad
headline: The pincers close in Tunisia
article: By the end of March the Axis forces in Tunisia were being squeezed from the west by the British First Army and the US II Corps, and from the south by the Eighth Army, which reached Gabès on 29 March. Patton's attempt to push through to the coast and cut off the retreating Axis forces was blocked in the hills around El Guettar and Maknassy. The Axis bridgehead was shrinking, and its supply line across the Sicilian Narrows was being cut by Allied aircraft and submarines. In Europe, Bomber Command was in the middle of the Battle of the Ruhr, a sustained campaign against the German industrial heartland.

episode: Mussolini is Tired of War
headline: Mussolini wants out
article: Mussolini met Hitler at Klessheim Castle near Salzburg from 7 to 10 April. Ill and depressed, he urged Hitler to make peace with Stalin so that the Axis could concentrate against the Western Allies in the Mediterranean. Hitler refused. Italy's war was going badly everywhere: its army in Russia had been destroyed, its African empire lost, its cities bombed, its navy hiding in port. Strikes broke out in Turin and Milan in March, the first mass strikes in Fascist Italy. Members of the Fascist leadership and the royal court were beginning to discuss removing Mussolini. In Tunisia, the Eighth Army broke through at Wadi Akarit on 6 April.

episode: Kursk - The Next Great Battle?
headline: Kursk: the next great battle
article: On 15 April Hitler issued Operation Order No. 6 for Operation Zitadelle, Citadel: a pincer attack from north and south to cut off the Kursk bulge and destroy the Soviet armies inside. He then postponed it repeatedly, waiting for new Tiger and Panther tanks. Soviet intelligence, from aerial reconnaissance, partisans and the British, revealed the plan. Stalin's generals persuaded him to stay on the defensive, absorb the attack and counterattack. The Soviets began digging an extraordinary system of defences: several belts of trenches, minefields and anti-tank strongpoints, up to 300 kilometres deep. The Germans could see them being built. The battle both sides were preparing would be fought on ground the defender had chosen.

episode: Ladies and Gentlemen, We Got Him - Yamamoto
headline: Yamamoto shot down
article: In April US codebreakers decoded a message giving the itinerary of Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, commander of Japan's Combined Fleet and architect of Pearl Harbor, for an inspection tour of front-line bases in the Solomons. On 18 April sixteen US Army P-38 fighters flew from Guadalcanal and intercepted his bomber near Bougainville; he was killed. The Japanese did not announce his death for a month. On 19 April in Warsaw, Jewish fighters in the ghetto began an armed uprising against the SS units sent to deport its remaining inhabitants, holding out for nearly a month against overwhelming force. On 13 April Germany announced the discovery of the Katyn graves.

episode: The race for Tunisia turns into a crawl
headline: The crawl toward Tunis
article: In late April Allied forces tried to break into the final Axis bridgehead around Tunis and Bizerte. The terrain of hills and ridges favoured the defence, and progress was slow. British troops fought for Longstop Hill, which fell on 26 April. The US II Corps, now under Omar Bradley since Patton left to plan Sicily, attacked through the hills toward Bizerte, taking Hill 609 on 30 April. On 25 April the Soviet Union broke off relations with the Polish government in London after it asked the Red Cross to investigate the Katyn massacres. Soviet officials blamed the Germans. The truth, that the NKVD had shot some 22,000 Polish officers and others in 1940, was not officially admitted by Moscow until 1990.

episode: Kilroy was Here! The fall of Tunis
headline: Tunis and Bizerte fall
article: On 6 May the Allies launched their final offensive, Operation Vulcan and then Strike, against the Tunis bridgehead. British armour broke through to Tunis on 7 May; the same day the Americans entered Bizerte. The Axis front collapsed. Axis troops fell back into the Cap Bon peninsula, but there was no evacuation; Allied navies and air forces had sealed the sea. American soldiers had a habit of leaving the graffiti "Kilroy was here" wherever they went, and it spread throughout North Africa. In the Pacific, American forces landed on Attu in the Aleutians on 11 May to retake it from Japan.

episode: The End of the War in Africa
headline: The war in Africa ends
article: On 13 May the last Axis forces in Tunisia surrendered. About 250,000 German and Italian soldiers went into captivity, a loss comparable to Stalingrad. General Alexander signalled Churchill: "We are masters of the North African shores." The Axis had lost an entire army group and much of its air transport fleet. On 16–17 May the RAF's 617 Squadron attacked dams in the Ruhr with bouncing bombs, breaching the Möhne and Eder dams; the floods killed about 1,600 people, many of them forced labourers. On 16 May SS General Jürgen Stroop reported that the Warsaw ghetto "no longer exists" and blew up the Great Synagogue.

episode: Wrapping up the North African Campaign
headline: Wrapping up North Africa
article: On 20 May the Allies held a victory parade in Tunis, with British, American and French troops marching past Eisenhower, Alexander and the French general Henri Giraud. Free French and former Vichy forces were slowly being merged into a single French army, though de Gaulle and Giraud were rivals for leadership. The Allies now had to decide where to go next. The British wanted to continue in the Mediterranean, through Sicily and Italy; the Americans wanted to focus on an invasion of France. At the Trident conference in Washington from 12 to 25 May, they agreed to invade Sicily and set a target date of May 1944 for crossing the Channel.

episode: Black May, Nazi Subs Defeated
headline: Black May: the U-boats are beaten
article: In May 1943 the Allies sank 41 U-boats, about a quarter of the operational fleet, while U-boat sinkings of merchant ships fell sharply. Convoy ONS 5 in early May was attacked by over 40 U-boats; its escorts sank six. Several factors came together: long-range Liberator aircraft closing the air gap, escort carriers, centimetric radar, support groups of escorts hunting U-boats, and Bletchley Park's renewed ability to read U-boat signals. On 24 May Admiral Dönitz, who lost his own son in May, withdrew his U-boats from the North Atlantic. Admiralty staff in Liverpool watched the plot change. The Battle of the Atlantic was not over, but it had been won.

episode: Banzai Charges in Alaska
headline: Banzai charge on Attu
article: On Attu, the westernmost of the Aleutian Islands, the American landing that began on 11 May turned into nearly three weeks of fighting in cold, fog and mud against a Japanese garrison of about 2,600. On 29 May, with no hope of relief, the surviving Japanese launched a massive banzai charge that broke through American lines before being destroyed. Fewer than 30 prisoners were taken.
