American losses were about 550 dead and many more from cold injuries. In Algiers, on 3 June, de Gaulle and Giraud formed the French Committee of National Liberation, a step toward a single French government in exile.

episode: Eisenhower Lays Out His Plans for Sicily
headline: Eisenhower plans Sicily
article: From his headquarters in Algiers, Eisenhower finalised plans for Operation Husky, the invasion of Sicily, scheduled for 10 July. The plan, after much argument, put Montgomery's Eighth Army ashore on the south-east coast and Patton's Seventh Army on the south-west coast, with Montgomery given the main role. British intelligence ran a deception, Operation Mincemeat, in which a corpse dressed as a Royal Marines officer, carrying false letters suggesting landings in Greece and Sardinia, was floated ashore in Spain; German intelligence took the bait. On 11 June the Italian island of Pantelleria surrendered after heavy bombing, before any troops landed. The real target, Sicily, was barely reinforced.

episode: Kursk: Soviets Dig-In for Blitzkrieg
headline: Kursk: the Soviets dig in
article: By mid-June the Soviet defences around Kursk were among the strongest ever built: around 5,000 kilometres of trenches, hundreds of thousands of mines, thousands of anti-tank guns organised in strongpoints, and reserves massed behind the bulge, including the Steppe Front under Ivan Konev. Hundreds of thousands of civilians helped dig them. The Germans massed almost 800,000 men and some 2,500 tanks and assault guns, including the new Panthers, which were plagued by mechanical problems. German generals were divided; Guderian argued the attack should be cancelled. Hitler admitted that the thought of the attack made his stomach turn, but kept it.

episode: Two Hundred Weeks of War
headline: Two hundred weeks of war
article: Two hundred weeks after the invasion of Poland, the shape of the war had changed. The Axis had lost in Africa and at Stalingrad and in the Atlantic. Germany still held most of Europe, but its cities were being bombed by the RAF at night and, increasingly, the US Eighth Air Force by day, under the Combined Bomber Offensive agreed at Casablanca. On 20–21 June RAF bombers attacked Friedrichshafen and flew on to bases in North Africa, the first "shuttle" raid. Inside occupied Europe, resistance was growing, and so were German reprisals. In June the Germans arrested Jean Moulin, de Gaulle's representative to the French Resistance. He died after torture.

episode: Tougher than Guadalcanal: New Georgia
headline: New Georgia: tougher than Guadalcanal
article: On 30 June American forces launched Operation Cartwheel, a two-pronged offensive aimed ultimately at isolating the great Japanese base at Rabaul. MacArthur's forces landed in New Guinea and the Trobriand Islands, and Admiral Halsey's forces landed on New Georgia in the central Solomons, aiming for the airfield at Munda. The New Georgia campaign turned into a slog through jungle and swamp against well-prepared Japanese defences. Inexperienced US Army divisions suffered heavily from combat stress and disease, and Munda did not fall until 5 August. In Europe, the German offensive at Kursk was days away. Each step toward Rabaul would cost more than planners expected.

episode: Kursk, When Titans Clash
headline: Kursk: when titans clash
photo: f:Bundesarchiv Bild 101I-219-0595-05, Russland, Kampf um Kursk.jpg
article: On 5 July the German Ninth Army attacked the northern face of the Kursk bulge and the Fourth Panzer Army and Army Detachment Kempf the southern face. Warned by intelligence of the exact time, Soviet artillery fired a pre-emptive barrage before the Germans started. In the north, the German attack stalled within days, advancing only about 12 kilometres into the Soviet defences. In the south, German panzer divisions, led by SS divisions, made deeper progress, pushing some 30 to 35 kilometres toward the village of Prokhorovka. Soviet tank losses were very heavy. On 10 July, before the outcome was clear, Allied forces landed in Sicily.

episode: Prokhorovka: An Avalanche of Armor
headline: Prokhorovka
article: On 12 July the Soviet Fifth Guards Tank Army counterattacked the II SS Panzer Corps near Prokhorovka, a railway station south of Kursk. Hundreds of Soviet tanks charged across open ground, some ramming German tanks. Soviet losses were very heavy, several times greater than German losses, but the German advance was stopped. Soviet histories later inflated it into the biggest tank battle in history, involving over a thousand tanks on each side; the real numbers were smaller. On the same day, the Soviets launched Operation Kutuzov against the German salient around Orel north of Kursk. On 13 July Hitler called off Citadel, partly citing the Sicily landings.

episode: Who Let the Dogs Out?! - The Invasion of Sicily
headline: The invasion of Sicily
article: On the night of 9–10 July Allied airborne troops dropped over Sicily in high winds, many scattered or drowned when gliders landed in the sea. At dawn eight divisions landed on the south and south-east coast, one of the largest amphibious operations of the war. Italian coastal divisions mostly collapsed, though some units fought hard; German armour counterattacked the American beachhead at Gela on 11 July and was stopped by naval gunfire. Allied ships accidentally shot down dozens of their own transport planes carrying paratroops over the invasion fleet. Syracuse fell on 10 July. Within days Italian morale in Sicily was crumbling.

episode: After a Victory at Kursk, The Soviets Attack Everywhere
headline: After Kursk, the Soviets attack everywhere
article: With Citadel called off, the Red Army went over to the offensive along much of the front. Operation Kutuzov drove into the Orel salient from the north and east, and on 17 July Soviet forces attacked on the Mius river and the Donets in the south to draw German reserves away. The Germans were short of men everywhere; the panzer divisions that had fought at Kursk were shuttled from crisis to crisis. In Sicily, Patton's Seventh Army swept west and took Palermo on 22 July, while Montgomery's advance up the east coast stalled at the foot of Mount Etna against German resistance. On 19 July Allied bombers struck railway yards in Rome for the first time.

episode: Mussolini Falls from Power
headline: Mussolini falls from power
photo: w:Fall of the Fascist regime in Italy
article: On the night of 24–25 July the Fascist Grand Council, meeting for the first time since 1939, voted 19 to 8 for a motion that effectively asked King Victor Emmanuel III to take back command of the armed forces. The next afternoon the king received Mussolini, told him he was dismissed, and had him arrested as he left. Marshal Pietro Badoglio became prime minister and announced that the war would go on at Germany's side; few believed it, least of all Hitler, who began moving divisions into Italy. Crowds celebrated in Italian cities. On the same night RAF bombers began Operation Gomorrah against Hamburg.

episode: Allied Tidal Wave in Romania
headline: The Ploiești raid and the Hamburg firestorm
article: On 1 August 177 US B-24 Liberators flew from Libya to bomb the Romanian oil refineries at Ploiești, which supplied much of Germany's oil, at extremely low altitude. Navigation errors and strong defences made it a costly raid: 53 aircraft were lost, and damage to the refineries was repaired within weeks. In Hamburg, the RAF raid on the night of 27–28 July had created a firestorm, a fire so intense it generated hurricane-force winds that sucked oxygen from shelters. Around 35,000 to 40,000 people died over the week of raids, most of them civilians. Germany's leaders were shaken. In Russia, Soviet troops took Orel and Belgorod on 5 August.

episode: Manstein Goes Great War Style
headline: Manstein's mobile defence
article: On 3 August the Red Army launched Operation Rumyantsev, the Belgorod–Kharkov offensive, against Manstein's Army Group South. Soviet tank armies broke through and drove toward Kharkov and the Dnieper. Manstein counterattacked with his remaining panzer divisions in a series of sharp actions around Bogodukhov, inflicting heavy losses on Soviet tank units, as he had in the Great War style of trading space for time. But he could only slow the advance. On 5 August Moscow celebrated the liberation of Orel and Belgorod with the first artillery salute of the war, a tradition that would be repeated hundreds of times. In Sicily, German forces began a skilled withdrawal across the Strait of Messina.

episode: Sicily Liberated; Italy in the Firing Line
headline: Sicily liberated; Italy next
article: Between 11 and 17 August German and Italian forces evacuated about 100,000 men and much of their equipment from Sicily across the Strait of Messina to the Italian mainland, protected by dense anti-aircraft guns. Patton's troops entered Messina on 17 August, just ahead of the British. The campaign had taken 38 days. It had also produced an ugly scandal when Patton slapped two soldiers suffering from combat stress in field hospitals. In Lisbon, Italian envoys were secretly negotiating an armistice with the Allies. On 17–18 August RAF bombers hit the German rocket research centre at Peenemünde on the Baltic coast.

episode: Kharkov Changes Hands for the Fourth Time
headline: Kharkov changes hands for the last time
article: On 23 August Soviet forces retook Kharkov for good. It was the fourth time the city had changed hands in the war, and much of it was in ruins. In the Donbas, Soviet armies broke through the German line on the Mius river. The German southern front was in danger of collapsing, and Manstein demanded the freedom to withdraw behind the Dnieper river. Hitler, who had ordered work started on an "Eastern Wall" defence line along the river, hesitated. In Quebec, Churchill and Roosevelt met at the Quadrant Conference, confirming Operation Overlord for May 1944, and agreeing to share atomic research.

episode: The War is Four Years Old this week
headline: Four years of war; the Allies land in Italy
article: On 3 September, the fourth anniversary of Britain's declaration of war, Montgomery's Eighth Army crossed the Strait of Messina and landed near Reggio Calabria at the toe of Italy, against little resistance. On the same day, in a tent at Cassibile in Sicily, Italian General Giuseppe Castellano secretly signed the armistice with the Allies. It would not be announced for five days. In the Soviet Union, the Red Army liberated Taganrog and broke into the Donbas. In the Pacific, Australian and American forces landed near Lae in New Guinea. The war was now four years old, and the Axis was retreating on every front.

episode: The Allies' Latest Victory
headline: Italy surrenders; landings at Salerno
article: On 8 September Eisenhower announced Italy's armistice. The next morning the US Fifth Army under Mark Clark landed at Salerno, south of Naples, and British troops landed at Taranto. Germany had prepared for Italy's surrender. In Operation Achse, German forces disarmed the Italian army in Italy, France, the Balkans and Greece within days, taking hundreds of thousands of prisoners. The king and Badoglio fled Rome for the south. The Italian fleet sailed for Malta to surrender; the Luftwaffe sank the battleship Roma with a guided bomb. At Salerno, German counterattacks nearly drove the Allies back into the sea. For several days the beachhead hung in the balance.

episode: Jailbreak! Mussolini on the Loose Again!
headline: Mussolini rescued from the Gran Sasso
article: On 12 September German paratroopers in gliders landed at the Campo Imperatore hotel on the Gran Sasso in the Abruzzo mountains, where Mussolini was being held, and flew him out in a light aircraft. SS officer Otto Skorzeny took much of the credit. Hitler set Mussolini up at the head of a puppet state in northern Italy, the Italian Social Republic, based at Salò on Lake Garda. On the Greek island of Cephalonia, German troops massacred thousands of Italian soldiers of the Acqui Division who had resisted being disarmed. At Salerno, Allied naval gunfire and airborne reinforcements saved the beachhead.

episode: Red Army Reaches the Dnieper
headline: The Red Army reaches the Dnieper
article: On 15 September Hitler finally authorised Army Group South to retreat behind the Dnieper. German forces withdrew, destroying what they could as they went in a scorched-earth policy. Soviet troops raced to reach the river before the Germans could organise defences, and from 22 September began crossing it on rafts, boats and anything that floated, seizing bridgeheads on the western bank. More than 2,000 soldiers were made Heroes of the Soviet Union for the Dnieper crossings. In Italy, the Allied armies linked up south of Salerno, and the Germans began withdrawing northward to defensive lines across the peninsula. The Eastern Wall existed mostly on paper.

episode: Smolensk and Naples Liberated! Both in ruins
headline: Smolensk and Naples liberated, both in ruins
article: On 25 September Soviet troops liberated Smolensk, a city that had been in German hands since July 1941; much of it had been destroyed. In Naples, citizens rose against the German occupiers in the "Four Days of Naples" from 27 to 30 September, partly to stop deportations of young men for forced labour. The Germans withdrew, wrecking the port, the water supply and public buildings, and planting time bombs. Allied troops entered on 1 October. In Corsica, Free French forces and local resistance liberated the island by early October, the first French department freed. In Denmark, most of the country's Jews were smuggled to Sweden in early October before a planned round-up.

episode: Could the Soviets Cut Off Crimea?
headline: Could the Soviets cut off Crimea?
article: In early October Soviet armies advanced in southern Ukraine toward the isthmus at Perekop, threatening to cut off German and Romanian forces in Crimea. Hitler insisted Crimea be held, partly to keep Soviet bombers away from the Romanian oil fields and to keep Romania and Turkey from wavering. German forces evacuated the Kuban bridgehead across the Kerch Strait from the Caucasus between September and early October. On 13 October Italy's Badoglio government declared war on Germany. In the Atlantic, the Allies began using bases in the Portuguese Azores in October, closing a gap in their air cover. Every month of delay in the south cost the Germans more men than they could replace.

episode: Zaporizhzhia!
headline: Zaporizhzhia
article: In mid-October the Red Army attacked the German bridgehead at Zaporizhzhia, a major industrial city on the Dnieper, which Hitler ordered held to protect the manganese mines at Nikopol. Soviet forces stormed the city in a night attack and took it on 14 October. The Germans had already blown up the great DnieproGES hydroelectric dam, once a showpiece of Soviet industrialisation. To the north, Soviet bridgeheads across the Dnieper near Kiev expanded. Behind the front, the Germans continued to deport civilians and destroy villages as they withdrew. In Italy, the US Fifth Army crossed the Volturno river on 13 October.

episode: Stalin Agrees to the United Nations
headline: Stalin agrees to a United Nations
article: At the Moscow Conference of foreign ministers from 18 October to 11 November, Cordell Hull, Anthony Eden and Vyacheslav Molotov agreed on a declaration calling for a general international organisation to maintain peace after the war, the seed of the United Nations. They also issued a declaration on Austria, calling it the first victim of Hitler's aggression, and a declaration on atrocities, warning Germans responsible for war crimes that they would be returned to the countries where they committed them for trial. China signed the Four Power Declaration. The Soviets were assured that the invasion of France would happen in spring 1944.

episode: Fresh German Armor in the USSR!
headline: Fresh German armour in the East
article: In late October the Germans counterattacked Soviet forces that had broken out of their Dnieper bridgeheads toward Krivoi Rog, the iron-ore centre, using fresh panzer divisions transferred from the west and Italy. The counterattack stopped the Soviet drive for a while and inflicted serious losses. But the Red Army had many more men and tanks, and its commanders were growing more skilful. Meanwhile, Soviet forces in the north broke through toward Nevel. The Wehrmacht was shifting forces from front to front to plug gaps, which meant that every new Allied landing or offensive pulled troops from somewhere else. The initiative stayed with the Red Army.

episode: Allies Launch new Phase in Pacific War
headline: A new phase in the Pacific war
article: On 1 November US Marines landed at Empress Augusta Bay on Bougainville in the northern Solomons, to build airfields within fighter range of Rabaul. The next night, a US cruiser force defeated a Japanese force sent to attack the landings. On 5 November and again on 11 November US carriers struck Rabaul and badly damaged Japanese cruisers there. The Allies decided not to invade Rabaul but to bypass and isolate it, letting its 100,000 troops wither. This "island-hopping" strategy would shape the rest of the Pacific war. Meanwhile Nimitz's Central Pacific force prepared to invade the Gilbert Islands. Japanese garrisons left behind were cut off and starved of supplies.

episode: Kiev Liberated! Celebrations in Moscow!
headline: Kiev liberated
article: On 6 November, the eve of the anniversary of the revolution, Soviet troops liberated Kiev. The main attack had come from a small bridgehead north of the city at Liutezh, where the Soviets had secretly moved a tank army. Moscow fired a 24-gun salute. The city was in ruins and much of its population had fled, been deported or been murdered; tens of thousands of Jews had been killed at Babi Yar in 1941. The Germans had tried in the weeks before to cover up the massacre by burning the bodies. A German counterattack in mid-November retook Zhitomir, but Kiev held. The Ukrainian capital was free after 778 days of occupation.

episode: A Conspiracy to kill America's President?
headline: A plot against the Big Three?
article: In late November Roosevelt and Churchill met Chiang Kai-shek in Cairo, then flew on to Tehran to meet Stalin for the first time. Before the conference Soviet security warned of a German plot to kill the Allied leaders, and Roosevelt was persuaded to stay at the Soviet embassy compound. A German plan, sometimes called Operation Long Jump, has been told in many versions; historians doubt it got beyond intelligence gossip, and some suspect the Soviets used the story to keep Roosevelt under their roof, where his rooms may have been bugged. What is certain is that the threat was taken seriously at the time.

episode: The Costliest Day in US Marine History
headline: Tarawa: the costliest day in Marine history
article: On 20 November the 2nd Marine Division landed on Betio, the main island of Tarawa atoll in the Gilberts. A low tide left landing craft stuck on the coral reef hundreds of metres from shore, and Marines had to wade in under heavy fire from Japanese bunkers. Over three days more than 1,000 Marines were killed and over 2,000 wounded on an island smaller than a large park; almost all of the 4,500 Japanese and Korean labourers died. Photographs and film of Tarawa shocked the American public. The Marines learned costly lessons in amphibious warfare that improved later landings. Makin was taken by the Army at the same time.

episode: Operation Overlord Confirmed at Teheran
headline: The Tehran Conference
article: The Big Three met in Tehran from 28 November to 1 December. Stalin pressed for a firm date for the invasion of France and got it: May 1944, with a supporting landing in southern France. In return he promised a Soviet offensive to coincide with it, and agreed to enter the war against Japan after Germany's defeat. They discussed, inconclusively, Germany's future and Poland's borders; Churchill illustrated with matchsticks how Poland might be moved westward. At a dinner, Stalin proposed shooting 50,000 German officers; Churchill walked out in anger. The Western Allies left committed to Overlord and the shape of postwar Europe began to emerge.

episode: An Amphibious Landing to take Rome?
headline: Toward Rome: the Gustav Line
article: In Italy, the Allied advance had become a slow, bloody crawl through mountains, rain and mud against successive German defensive lines. Field Marshal Kesselring had persuaded Hitler that Italy could be defended south of Rome, and the main line, the Gustav Line, ran across the narrowest part of the peninsula, anchored on the Garigliano and Rapido rivers and the town of Cassino. British and Canadian troops fought on the Adriatic side; Americans and British on the west. Allied planners began considering an amphibious landing behind the Gustav Line, near Anzio, to break the deadlock. Eisenhower was named supreme commander for Overlord on 7 December.

episode: A Super Bomber to Break Japan
headline: A super bomber to break Japan
article: By late 1943 the US Army Air Forces had a new aircraft, the Boeing B-29 Superfortress: pressurised, long-ranged and carrying a heavy bomb load. Its development had been troubled, with engine fires and production problems, and cost more than the atomic bomb project. The plan was to base it first in India and China and strike Japan from there; later, once the Marianas were taken, from Saipan and Guam. American planners saw it as a way to bomb Japan's cities and industries from the air. In Europe, the US Eighth Air Force was suffering heavy losses in daylight raids over Germany and waiting for long-range escort fighters.

episode: Stalin's Christmas Surprise - Major Offensives to Come
headline: Stalin's Christmas offensive
article: On 24 December the First Ukrainian Front launched the Zhitomir–Berdichev offensive west of Kiev, breaking through German lines and driving toward the pre-war Polish border. It was the first of a series of winter offensives planned along the entire southern front. On 26 December, in the Barents Sea, British warships sank the battlecruiser Scharnhorst in the Battle of the North Cape as she tried to attack an Arctic convoy; only 36 of her crew of nearly 2,000 survived. Eisenhower was confirmed as supreme commander, with Montgomery as ground commander for the invasion. In Italy, the Allies fought for Ortona on the Adriatic.

episode: Canadians Take Little Stalingrad
headline: Canadians take "Little Stalingrad"
article: In December the 1st Canadian Division fought for the small Adriatic town of Ortona, defended by German paratroopers. The fighting through narrow streets and stone houses was so intense that the press called it "Little Stalingrad". Canadians developed "mouse-holing", blasting through walls from house to house rather than going into the streets. The Germans withdrew on 28 December. The battle cost the Canadians over 1,300 casualties in December. Further west, Allied troops were bogged down in front of the Gustav Line. As 1943 ended, the war in Italy had become a symbol of how expensive the Mediterranean strategy had grown.

episode: Ep 228 - "Russians 27 miles from Poland!"
headline: The Red Army reaches the old Polish border
article: In the first week of January Soviet troops of the First Ukrainian Front crossed the pre-1939 Polish–Soviet border near Sarny, in territory the USSR had annexed in 1939 and regarded as its own. The Polish government in London insisted on its 1939 borders; Stalin demanded the Curzon Line, roughly the 1939 Nazi–Soviet partition line. The question of Poland's future became urgent in Allied diplomacy. The Red Army's advance in Ukraine continued despite the winter and mud. In Britain, Eisenhower and Montgomery arrived to take command of the invasion forces and immediately insisted the landing be widened from three divisions to five.

episode: Ep 229 - Time to Liberate Leningrad!
headline: Time to free Leningrad
article: On 14 January the Leningrad and Volkhov Fronts launched a major offensive from the Oranienbaum bridgehead west of the city and from Leningrad itself, and from the Volkhov river toward Novgorod. The German Eighteenth Army was well dug in after more than two years of siege, but it had been weakened by transfers to other fronts. After days of heavy fighting, the Soviet attacks broke through. In Italy, the Allied armies prepared to attack the Gustav Line around Cassino in support of the planned landing at Anzio. In the Pacific, Australian and American troops pushed along the north coast of New Guinea.

episode: Ep 230 - Monte Cassino, the Battle Begins
headline: Monte Cassino: the battle begins
article: On 17 January the British X Corps attacked across the Garigliano river on the western end of the Gustav Line. On 20–21 January the US 36th Division tried to cross the Rapido river below Cassino and was cut to pieces, losing some 1,700 men in two days; it became one of the most controversial American actions of the war. The town of Cassino and the mountain above it, crowned by the ancient Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, dominated the valley that led to Rome. Kesselring's forces held strong positions on the heights. In Leningrad, Soviet forces linked up between the city and the Oranienbaum bridgehead on 19–20 January.

episode: Anzio Begins - Allies Already Pinned Down
headline: Anzio: the Allies land and stop
article: On 22 January the US VI Corps under General John Lucas landed at Anzio and Nettuno, about 50 kilometres south of Rome, achieving complete surprise. Lucas spent the next days consolidating his beachhead rather than pushing inland toward the Alban Hills, as he had been told to secure his position. Kesselring reacted quickly, rushing reserves to seal off the beachhead, and soon German forces outnumbered the Allies there. Churchill, who had championed the landing, complained: "I had hoped that we were hurling a wildcat onto the shore, but all we got was a stranded whale." The Allies would be pinned down at Anzio for four months.

episode: Leningrad: NO STEP BACK!
headline: The siege of Leningrad is over
article: On 27 January the Soviet command declared that the siege of Leningrad had been completely lifted, 872 days after it began. Leningrad fired a 324-gun salute, the first time a city other than Moscow had been given the honour. German forces were driven back toward the Luga river and eventually to the Panther Line on the old Estonian border. The cost to the city had been immense: perhaps a million civilians dead, most from starvation and cold, and much of its architecture destroyed. At Anzio, German counterattacks began. At Cassino, the US 34th Division gained a foothold in the hills north of the town and fought its way close to the monastery.

episode: German Desperation in Korsun Pocket
headline: The Korsun pocket
article: On 28 January Soviet forces closed a ring around two German corps, about 60,000 men, near Korsun and Cherkassy in central Ukraine, west of the Dnieper. Hitler again forbade a breakout and ordered relief attacks, which ground forward in the mud. The Luftwaffe tried to supply the pocket by air. Soviet propaganda and the "Free Germany" committee of captured German officers appealed to the trapped troops to surrender. In the Marshall Islands, US forces took Kwajalein in early February in an operation that showed lessons from Tarawa had been learned. In Italy, at Cassino, New Zealand and Indian troops prepared to take over the attack.

episode: The Destruction of Monte Cassino
headline: The destruction of Monte Cassino abbey
article: On 15 February over 200 Allied bombers destroyed the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, founded in the sixth century. Allied commanders, especially the New Zealand corps commander Bernard Freyberg, believed the Germans were using it as an observation post; they were not, though they had positions close to it. Several hundred Italian civilians sheltering inside were killed. German paratroopers then occupied the ruins, which made excellent defensive positions. The ground attacks that followed failed. On 16–17 February, about 30,000 Germans broke out of the Korsun pocket under fire and in snow, losing their heavy equipment and many men. At Anzio, a major German counteroffensive began.

episode: Tojo Takes Control
headline: Tojo takes control; Truk smashed
article: On 17–18 February US carrier aircraft attacked Truk, the main Japanese naval base in the central Pacific, sinking dozens of merchant ships and several warships and destroying hundreds of aircraft. The base, sometimes called Japan's Pearl Harbor, was neutralised. Days later, on 21 February, Prime Minister Hideki Tojo took the additional post of chief of the army general staff, concentrating military and political authority in his own hands in an attempt to take control of the faltering war. In Europe, Allied bombers launched "Big Week" from 20 February, a series of raids on German aircraft factories that drew the Luftwaffe into battle with American escort fighters.

episode: MacArthur and Nimitz Go Head-to-Head
headline: MacArthur and Nimitz go head to head
article: On 29 February MacArthur sent troops to land on Los Negros in the Admiralty Islands, on reports that the islands were lightly held. They were not, and the landing was nearly overwhelmed, but it held, and the capture of the Admiralties completed the isolation of Rabaul. In Washington, the Joint Chiefs had to arbitrate between MacArthur's push along New Guinea toward the Philippines and Nimitz's drive across the central Pacific toward the Marianas. They decided both would continue. In Italy, the German counteroffensive at Anzio failed by early March with heavy losses. In the USSR, the Red Army prepared new offensives in the western Ukraine.

episode: Zhukov Hits the Ground Running
headline: Zhukov hits the ground running
article: On 4 March the First Ukrainian Front, now commanded by Zhukov after the fatal wounding of General Vatutin by Ukrainian nationalist insurgents, launched a new offensive in the western Ukraine, despite the spring thaw that turned the roads into mud. Soviet tanks, with wide tracks, and American-built trucks supplied under Lend-Lease coped better with the mud than the Germans. Further south, Konev's Second Ukrainian Front attacked toward the Romanian border. The German front in the south began to break up. On 6 March the US Eighth Air Force made its first major daylight raid on Berlin. In Burma, the second Chindit expedition under Orde Wingate flew into Japanese-held territory.

episode: The Japanese Invade India!
headline: Japan invades India
article: On 8 March the Japanese 15th Army under General Renya Mutaguchi crossed the Chindwin river into India, aiming to destroy the British and Indian forces at Imphal and Kohima and seize their supply bases. Units of the Indian National Army, made up of former Indian prisoners of war who now fought with Japan, joined the offensive. The Japanese plan relied on capturing British supplies because it had few of its own. General William Slim's Fourteenth Army pulled back to Imphal and Kohima, supplied by air. In Europe, the Germans had to deal with Hungary, which was secretly trying to leave the war.

episode: Germany Invades Hungary
headline: Germany occupies Hungary
article: Hitler had learned that Hungary's regent, Admiral Miklós Horthy, was secretly negotiating with the Allies. He summoned Horthy to Klessheim Castle, and while Horthy was away on 19 March German troops occupied Hungary in Operation Margarethe. A pro-German government was installed. Hungary's Jews, about 800,000 people, had suffered discrimination and forced labour but most had escaped deportation until now. Adolf Eichmann arrived in Budapest with his staff. Between mid-May and early July, around 437,000 Hungarian Jews were deported, almost all to Auschwitz-Birkenau, where most were murdered on arrival. In the Pacific, US forces were advancing along New Guinea. It was one of the fastest deportations of the Holocaust.

episode: Goodbye Manstein… Hello Model
headline: Goodbye Manstein, hello Model
article: In late March the Soviets encircled the German First Panzer Army, around 200,000 men, near Kamenets-Podolsky. Manstein, defying Hitler, ordered it to break out to the west instead of south, and it succeeded in escaping in April. On 30 March Hitler dismissed Manstein and Ewald von Kleist, his two most senior commanders in the south, replacing Manstein with Walter Model, known as a ruthless and energetic defender. Army Group South was renamed Army Group North Ukraine. On 24–25 March, 76 Allied airmen escaped from the Stalag Luft III prisoner of war camp; 50 recaptured men were murdered by the Gestapo.

episode: New Offensive in the Crimea
headline: A new offensive in Crimea
article: On 8 April the Soviet Fourth Ukrainian Front attacked the German and Romanian Seventeenth Army in Crimea, breaking through the Perekop isthmus and the Sivash lagoon. At the same time Soviet forces attacked from the Kerch peninsula in the east. Hitler again ordered Crimea held. Simferopol fell on 13 April. The Germans and Romanians fell back toward Sevastopol, where Germans had fought their way in two years before. In the west, Soviet troops crossed into Romania. In the occupied Netherlands, preparations for a German defence of the coast continued. In Britain, the invasion forces were rehearsing landings on the south coast.

episode: 4,000 German Teens Trapped in Tarnopol
headline: Trapped in Tarnopol
article: Hitler declared a number of cities in the path of the Soviet advance to be "fortresses" to be held at all costs. One was Tarnopol in western Ukraine, where about 4,600 German troops, many of them young and inexperienced, were surrounded in March. They held until 15 April; a relief attempt failed, and only around 55 men reached German lines. The "fortress" policy tied down troops who could have been used elsewhere and condemned many of them. In the Pacific, MacArthur's forces landed at Hollandia in New Guinea on 22 April, far behind Japanese lines. At Kohima, the British garrison was holding against Japanese attacks around the deputy commissioner's tennis court.

episode: The Biggest Offensive in Japanese History
headline: The biggest Japanese offensive of the war
article: In April Japan launched Operation Ichi-Go, the largest offensive in its history, with around 500,000 men. Its aims were to open a land route from Manchuria to Indochina and to destroy the US air bases in southern China from which American bombers could strike Japan. The first phase, in Henan province, rolled over Nationalist forces weakened by years of war, inflation and a terrible famine in 1942–43 that had killed millions. Chinese armies retreated, sometimes in panic, and were attacked by peasants angry at their requisitioning. Chiang Kai-shek's standing with the Americans sank. In Burma, the Kohima battle continued. It would be Japan's last major victory on land.

episode: Germany's Existential Crisis
headline: Germany's existential crisis
photo: w:Strategic bombing during World War II
article: By spring 1944 Germany was fighting on three fronts and losing on all of them. Allied bombers were striking its cities around the clock, and the Luftwaffe's fighter force was being destroyed by American long-range escorts. Its oil refineries and synthetic fuel plants were about to become targets. Its armies were short of men; boys and older men were being drafted. Hitler still hoped that defeating the coming invasion in the west would allow him to shift forces east. Albert Speer had increased armaments production remarkably, partly using forced labour on a huge scale, but it could not match the combined production of the Allies.

episode: Total Chaos on the Chinese Front!
headline: Chaos on the Chinese front
article: In late April and May Japan's Ichi-Go offensive drove through Henan, capturing Luoyang in late May. Nationalist forces collapsed in many places; the Japanese suffered relatively few losses. American officers, including Stilwell, blamed Chiang Kai-shek's leadership and the corruption of his regime; Chiang blamed the lack of Allied supplies. Meanwhile in northern Burma, Chinese and American troops under Stilwell, with Merrill's Marauders, pushed toward Myitkyina, an important airfield and railway junction. In India, the Japanese siege of Kohima and Imphal was faltering as their supplies ran out and the monsoon approached. For the Chinese people, 1944 was among the worst years of the war, and the regime's credibility suffered badly.

episode: Victory at Sevastopol!
headline: Sevastopol liberated
article: On 9 May Soviet forces liberated Sevastopol after a short but fierce assault. Hitler had ordered the remnants of the Seventeenth Army to hold, and then permitted a late evacuation; thousands of German and Romanian soldiers were killed or captured on the Chersonese peninsula while waiting for ships. Crimea was free of Axis forces by 12 May. Within days, the NKVD deported the entire Crimean Tatar population, nearly 200,000 people, to Central Asia, accusing them of collaboration; many thousands died during the deportation and the following years. In Italy, the Allies launched Operation Diadem, a renewed offensive against the Gustav Line, on 11 May.

episode: The Fall of Monte Cassino
headline: The fall of Monte Cassino
article: Operation Diadem began on the night of 11–12 May with an attack by British, American, French, Polish, Canadian and Indian forces along the Gustav Line. French colonial troops, many of them Moroccan mountain soldiers, broke through the Aurunci Mountains, outflanking the German defences; they also committed many rapes against Italian civilians, which caused lasting bitterness. On 18 May soldiers of the Polish II Corps raised the Polish flag over the ruins of Monte Cassino abbey after a week of bloody fighting. The road to Rome through the Liri valley was opening. At Kohima, British and Indian troops cleared the last Japanese from the ridge in mid-May.

episode: Breakout from Anzio!
headline: Breakout from Anzio
article: On 23 May the US VI Corps, now commanded by Lucian Truscott, broke out of the Anzio beachhead. The plan was to drive east to Valmontone and cut off the German Tenth Army retreating from the Gustav Line. On 25 May, troops from Anzio and the main front linked up. Then General Mark Clark, commander of the Fifth Army, turned the bulk of his forces north toward Rome rather than east to cut off the retreating Germans. Much of the German army escaped to fight again on lines further north. Clark wanted his army to be first into Rome. Historians have argued about the decision ever since.

episode: The Allies are Driving for Rome
headline: The drive for Rome
article: In the last days of May the US Fifth Army pushed toward Rome through the Alban Hills, while the Germans fell back to avoid being cut off. Kesselring declared Rome an open city and withdrew. In Britain, the invasion forces were sealed into their camps, and the invasion fleet of thousands of ships began to assemble along the south coast. Weather forecasts for early June were bad. The German high command still believed the main invasion would come in the Pas-de-Calais, thanks partly to an elaborate deception, Operation Fortitude, which included a fictional army group under Patton. Rome was within reach and Normandy days away.

episode: The Invasion of Normandy begins!
bigboard: Rome liberated; D-Day: the Normandy landings
headline: Rome liberated; D-Day in Normandy
photo: f:Into the Jaws of Death 23-0455M edit.jpg
article: American troops entered Rome on 4 June. Two days later, on 6 June, the Allies landed in Normandy. Overnight, three airborne divisions dropped behind the beaches. At dawn, after heavy bombing and naval bombardment, five divisions landed: Americans at Utah and Omaha, British at Gold and Sword, Canadians at Juno. At Omaha, the Americans suffered heavy losses before getting off the beach. By nightfall some 156,000 Allied troops were ashore, at a cost of about 10,000 casualties, including more than 4,000 dead. The beachheads had not yet linked up and the city of Caen, an objective for the first day, was still in German hands. The German command, convinced this was a diversion, held back reserves.

episode: Titanic Clash Looms In Pacific
bigboard: First V-1 flying bombs hit London
headline: The first flying bombs hit London
article: On the night of 12–13 June the first German V-1 flying bombs, pilotless jet-propelled missiles launched from ramps in northern France, fell on London. Within weeks thousands were being fired; they killed over 6,000 people in Britain by the end of the war and drove a new wave of evacuation from the capital. Fighters, anti-aircraft guns and barrage balloons brought down many. In Normandy, the five beachheads had linked up, but the Germans were holding around Caen. In the Pacific, US forces landed on Saipan in the Marianas on 15 June, and the Japanese fleet sailed to give battle, setting up the largest carrier battle in history.

episode: The Greatest Pincer Movement in Military History
headline: Operation Bagration
article: On 22 June, three years to the day after Barbarossa, the Red Army launched Operation Bagration against German Army Group Centre in Belarus. Some 1.7 million Soviet troops, with thousands of tanks and aircraft, struck a German front that had been stripped of reserves because the high command expected the main blow in Ukraine. Soviet deception had worked. Partisans blew up railway lines behind German lines before the offensive. In the Philippine Sea on 19–20 June, American carrier pilots shot down hundreds of Japanese aircraft in what they called the "Great Marianas Turkey Shoot"; three Japanese carriers were sunk. The scale and speed of the attack took the German command completely by surprise.

episode: Allies Liberate Cherbourg
headline: Cherbourg falls
article: On 26 June the German commander in Cherbourg surrendered to the US VII Corps, giving the Allies a deep-water port. The Germans had wrecked the harbour so thoroughly that it took weeks to open; in the meantime, the Allies relied on the beaches and an artificial Mulberry harbour at Arromanches, after a storm from 19 to 22 June had wrecked the American Mulberry at Omaha. In Belarus, Bagration was destroying Army Group Centre: Vitebsk, Mogilev and Bobruisk were surrounded and fell in quick succession. Hitler's orders to hold "fortified places" again condemned the troops in them. In the Pacific, the fighting on Saipan continued.

episode: The Destruction of Army Group Center
headline: The destruction of Army Group Centre
article: On 3 July the Red Army liberated Minsk, the capital of Belarus, closing a pocket east of the city that trapped about 100,000 German troops. In less than two weeks, Army Group Centre had lost around 28 divisions. It was the worst defeat in German military history, larger than Stalingrad. On 17 July some 57,000 German prisoners were marched through the streets of Moscow, followed by street-cleaning trucks to "wash" the roads behind them. In Normandy, British and Canadian forces attacked Caen, and US forces fought through the bocage, the hedgerow country, where small gains came at high cost. The road to Poland and East Prussia lay open.

episode: Mass Suicide on Saipan
headline: Saipan falls, and its civilians die
article: The battle for Saipan ended on 9 July after more than three weeks of fighting. On 7 July several thousand Japanese troops made the largest banzai charge of the war, overrunning American positions before being destroyed. Almost the entire Japanese garrison of about 30,000 died. Thousands of Japanese civilians, told by propaganda that the Americans would torture and kill them, killed themselves, many by jumping from the cliffs at the island's northern tip, despite American appeals through loudspeakers. American losses were about 3,000 dead. Saipan put Tokyo within range of B-29s. In Normandy, British and Canadian troops took most of Caen on 9 July, much of it destroyed by bombing.

episode: Sayonara Tojo
headline: The July plot against Hitler; Tojo falls
article: On 20 July Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg left a bomb in a briefcase under the map table at Hitler's headquarters in East Prussia. It exploded, killing four people, but Hitler survived with minor injuries; the heavy table had shielded him. In Berlin, the conspirators' attempt to seize power collapsed within hours. Stauffenberg and others were shot that night. Thousands were arrested in the following weeks and around 200 executed, many after show trials. Rommel, implicated, was forced to take poison in October. In Tokyo, Hideki Tojo's government resigned on 18 July after the fall of Saipan. In Normandy, Operation Goodwood east of Caen gained little at the cost of hundreds of tanks.

episode: Bradley Unleashes His Cobra
bigboard: Operation Cobra breaks out of Normandy
headline: Operation Cobra breaks out of Normandy
article: On 25 July, after a day's delay and two bombing raids that killed over 100 American soldiers, including General Lesley McNair, by bombs falling short, the US First Army attacked west of Saint-Lô in Operation Cobra. Bombers carpeted a narrow strip of the German front with high explosive, and the German Panzer Lehr Division was virtually destroyed. By 27 July American armour was through the German line and racing south. Coutances fell on 28 July and Avranches, the gateway to Brittany, on 30 July. The stalemate in Normandy was broken. In the east, Soviet forces reached the Vistula and liberated Lublin; nearby they found the Majdanek camp.

episode: The Warsaw Uprising Begins!
headline: The Warsaw Uprising
article: On 1 August the Polish Home Army rose against the German occupiers of Warsaw, timing it as the Red Army approached the city from the east. It aimed to liberate the capital before the Soviets arrived so that Poland's government in London, not Moscow's Polish Committee of National Liberation, could greet them. About 40,000 fighters, poorly armed, took much of the city in the first days. The Red Army halted on the Vistula; Stalin refused for weeks to let Allied planes use Soviet airfields to drop supplies. The Germans brought in SS and police units, and in the district of Wola they massacred tens of thousands of civilians in the first week. In France, Patton's Third Army was activated and swept into Brittany.

episode: Panzer Revenge in Normandy
headline: Hitler's counterattack at Mortain
article: On the night of 6–7 August, on Hitler's orders, German panzer divisions counterattacked near Mortain, aiming to reach the coast at Avranches and cut off Patton's army. Warned by Ultra intelligence, the Allies were ready. The US 30th Division held Hill 314 above Mortain for six days, surrounded, and Allied fighter-bombers attacked the German armour in daylight. The attack failed. It also pushed German forces further west, into a pocket that was forming between the Americans advancing from the south and the Canadians and Poles pushing from Caen toward Falaise. On 8 August, Canadian forces began Operation Totalize south of Caen.

episode: Hitler Has a Bad Day
headline: Dragoon lands in Provence; the Falaise pocket closes
article: On 15 August American and French forces landed on the Riviera coast of Provence in Operation Dragoon. Resistance was light. French troops took Toulon and Marseille within two weeks, giving the Allies two big ports. In Normandy, the gap at Falaise was narrowing: Canadian and Polish forces from the north and Americans from the south closed it on 19–21 August. Tens of thousands of Germans escaped, but around 50,000 were captured and the roads in the pocket were choked with destroyed vehicles and dead horses. Field Marshal Günther von Kluge, recalled to Berlin after he lost contact with his headquarters, killed himself. Hitler had a very bad week.

episode: The War is Five Years Old
headline: Five years of war; Paris is free
photo: f:Crowds of French patriots line the Champs Elysees-edit2.jpg
article: The Paris Resistance rose on 19 August, and on 24–25 August the French 2nd Armoured Division of General Leclerc, with the US 4th Infantry Division, entered the city. The German commander, General Dietrich von Choltitz, surrendered on 25 August, having ignored Hitler's orders to destroy the city. De Gaulle walked down the Champs-Élysées the next day to huge crowds. The war was five years old. Romania changed sides on 23 August after a coup by King Michael; the Soviets took the Ploiești oil fields on 30 August. In Slovakia, a national uprising began on 29 August. Allied armies raced across northern France toward the Seine and beyond.

episode: Bulgaria at War with Everyone
headline: Brussels liberated; Bulgaria switches sides
article: On 3 September British tanks of the Guards Armoured Division entered Brussels to scenes of wild celebration, after an advance of over 300 kilometres in less than a week. Antwerp, with its great port intact, fell the next day, but the Scheldt estuary connecting it to the sea remained in German hands, making it useless for months. Allied supply lines from Normandy were stretched to breaking point. The Soviet Union declared war on Bulgaria on 5 September; Bulgaria, after a coup on 9 September, declared war on Germany. The first V-2 rockets hit Paris and London on 8 September; unlike the V-1, they could not be intercepted.

episode: The Ballad of Chiang and Vinegar Joe
headline: Chiang and "Vinegar Joe"
article: In China, the Ichi-Go offensive had pushed into Hunan and Guangxi, capturing Changsha and laying siege to Hengyang, which fell in August after a long defence. American air bases were overrun. Roosevelt, under pressure from Stilwell, sent Chiang Kai-shek a blunt message in September demanding that Stilwell be given command of all Chinese forces. Stilwell, known as "Vinegar Joe", delivered it personally and with obvious satisfaction. Chiang, humiliated, demanded his recall. Roosevelt gave way and Stilwell was recalled in October. On the Western Front, Allied forces reached the German border near Aachen, and Patton's Third Army crossed the Moselle. China's war effort remained a source of friction between the allies.

episode: Operation Market Garden Begins
headline: Operation Market Garden
article: On 17 September the Allies launched Operation Market Garden, Montgomery's plan to use three airborne divisions to seize a string of bridges across rivers and canals in the Netherlands, opening a road for British armour to cross the Rhine at Arnhem and outflank the Siegfried Line. American paratroopers took bridges at Eindhoven and Nijmegen after hard fighting; the British 1st Airborne Division landed near Arnhem, far from its objective, and only one battalion under John Frost reached the road bridge. Two SS panzer divisions refitting nearby, which intelligence had warned of, reacted quickly. The ground advance along a single road fell behind schedule.

episode: The End of Market Garden
headline: The end of Market Garden
article: Frost's battalion held the north end of the Arnhem bridge for four days before being overwhelmed on 21 September. The rest of the 1st Airborne Division was pushed into a perimeter at Oosterbeek, under constant shelling. On the night of 25–26 September, about 2,400 men were evacuated across the Rhine; nearly 7,000 were captured or killed. Market Garden had failed, and with it the hope of ending the war in 1944. Montgomery claimed it was "90 per cent successful". The Dutch railway strike that began in support of the operation led the Germans to block food supplies to the western Netherlands, contributing to the "Hunger Winter" in which some 20,000 people died.

episode: The End of the Warsaw Uprising
headline: The end of the Warsaw Uprising
article: On 2 October, after 63 days of fighting, the Home Army in Warsaw capitulated. The Germans agreed to treat its fighters as prisoners of war. About 16,000 insurgents and up to 200,000 civilians had died, many murdered in massacres. The survivors among the city's civilians were expelled, and Hitler ordered the city razed. German demolition squads blew up building after building in the following months. The Red Army, a few kilometres away across the Vistula, did not intervene. Late, limited Soviet and Allied air drops had made little difference. For Poles, the uprising became a symbol of courage and of betrayal by allies.

episode: The Isolation of Army Group North
headline: Army Group North is isolated
article: On 10 October Soviet troops reached the Baltic coast near Memel, cutting off German Army Group North in Courland, in western Latvia. Riga fell on 13 October. Around 200,000 German troops would remain trapped in the Courland pocket until the end of the war, supplied by sea, because Hitler refused to evacuate them. In Greece, German forces withdrew from Athens on 12 October, and British troops landed. In Moscow, Churchill met Stalin on 9 October and proposed the "percentages agreement", jotting on a sheet of paper how much influence each power would have in Romania, Greece, Bulgaria, Hungary and Yugoslavia.

episode: SS Commando Coup in Hungary
bigboard: Belgrade liberated; Aachen, the first German city to fall
headline: Belgrade freed; Aachen falls; a coup in Budapest
article: On 20 October Soviet troops and Tito's Partisans liberated Belgrade. On 21 October the German garrison of Aachen surrendered to the US First Army after three weeks of fighting. It was the first German city to fall to the Western Allies. On 15 October Hungary's Horthy announced on the radio that Hungary had asked the Soviets for an armistice. German commandos under Otto Skorzeny kidnapped his son and forced him to resign. The fascist Arrow Cross party under Ferenc Szálasi took power. Its militias began murdering Jews in Budapest, and death marches of Jews toward Austria began. On 20 October American troops landed on Leyte in the Philippines.

episode: The Battle of Leyte Gulf
headline: The Battle of Leyte Gulf
article: From 23 to 26 October the Japanese navy threw almost everything it had left against the American landings at Leyte in a set of battles known together as Leyte Gulf, the largest naval battle in history. Japanese carriers, nearly empty of aircraft, lured Halsey's main fleet north, while two battleship forces converged on the landing area. One was destroyed in the Surigao Strait; the other, including the giant battleship Yamato, surprised a weak force of escort carriers and destroyers off Samar, which fought desperately, before inexplicably turning back. The Japanese lost four carriers, three battleships and many other ships. The first organised kamikaze attacks were made on 25 October.

episode: Stalin Says, "Bring Me Budapest!"
headline: Stalin wants Budapest; the Hürtgen Forest
article: On 29 October Soviet and Romanian forces launched an offensive toward Budapest. Stalin, eager to take the city before the Western Allies could influence events in central Europe, pressed his commanders for speed. In the west, the US First Army pushed into the Hürtgen Forest south-east of Aachen, a dense, hilly pine forest full of German bunkers, minefields and pre-registered artillery. Fighting there had begun in September; a new attack in early November by the 28th Division at Schmidt ended in disaster. Trees shattered by shellfire sent splinters flying, and American advantages in armour and air power counted for little. In the Netherlands, Canadian troops fought to clear the Scheldt estuary.

episode: The Futile Fight in Hurtgen Forest
headline: The futile fight in the Hürtgen
article: The American attack on the village of Schmidt in early November was thrown back by German counterattacks; the 28th Infantry Division lost over 6,000 men in two weeks. The Hürtgen battle would continue into December, costing the Americans some 30,000 casualties for limited gains. In the Netherlands, the Allies finished clearing the Scheldt estuary on 8 November, after the Canadians and British fought through flooded polders and Walcheren Island. On 7 November Roosevelt was elected to a fourth term. On 12 November RAF Lancasters sank the battleship Tirpitz in a Norwegian fjord with "Tallboy" bombs; around 1,000 of her crew died.

episode: How Himmler Learned to Love the Russians
headline: Himmler looks for a way out
article: As defeat approached, some Nazi leaders began to seek ways out. Heinrich Himmler, head of the SS and responsible for the genocide of the Jews, ordered in late November that the gassing at Auschwitz be stopped and the crematoria dismantled, partly to destroy evidence. Through intermediaries in Switzerland and Sweden, he explored contacts with the Western Allies and with Jewish organisations, hoping to save himself. The murder of Jews did not end; it moved into death marches and camps inside Germany. The Volkssturm, a militia of boys and older men, was announced on 18 October. In France, the First French Army reached the Rhine near Basel.

episode: General Patton's Metz Obsession
headline: Patton and Metz
article: In November Patton's Third Army attacked the fortress city of Metz, ringed by forts from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The autumn campaign in Lorraine, through rain and mud, was slow and costly; the Third Army suffered heavily from trench foot as well as German fire. Metz itself fell on 22 November, although some forts held out until December. Further south, French forces liberated Strasbourg on 23 November, fulfilling an oath sworn by Leclerc in 1941 at Kufra in the Libyan desert. In Germany, Hitler was secretly preparing a major offensive in the Ardennes. Lorraine became a byword for slow, grinding attrition and miserable weather.

episode: Was Hürtgen Forest Worth it?
headline: Antwerp opens; was the Hürtgen worth it?
article: On 28 November the first Allied convoy reached Antwerp, after minesweepers had cleared the 80-kilometre Scheldt channel. The port could now unload tens of thousands of tons a day, close to the front. The Germans attacked it with V-1s and V-2s; Antwerp would be hit by more V-weapons than any other city. In the Hürtgen Forest, the Americans were still fighting; the forest dams on the Roer river, which the Germans could open to flood the valley, were a major objective that had been overlooked at first. Historians have argued whether the whole battle was necessary. In Greece, fighting broke out between British troops and communist-led resistance in Athens.

episode: Can the Americans Stop the Kamikazes?
headline: Can the Americans stop the kamikazes?
article: In late 1944 Japanese pilots began deliberately crashing their aircraft into American ships off the Philippines. The kamikaze "special attack units" were made up mostly of young men with little training. They damaged or sank many ships, including carriers, and their attacks spread fear among American sailors. The US Navy developed new defensive tactics, including radar picket ships and more anti-aircraft guns. On Leyte, the American ground campaign was slower than planned. In Europe, in the Ardennes, the Germans were massing three armies in the forests, while the American divisions in front of them were resting or inexperienced. The weapon was born of desperation, and it worked often enough to frighten.

episode: The Battle of the Bulge Begins
headline: The Battle of the Bulge begins
photo: f:American soldiers of the 289th Infantry Regiment march along the road to cut off the St. Vith-Houffalize road in Belgium, January 24, 1945.jpg
s:Battle of the Bulge 1944 snow soldiers
article: On 16 December three German armies attacked through the Ardennes in Belgium and Luxembourg, aiming to cross the Meuse and take Antwerp, splitting the Allies. They struck a quiet sector held by four American divisions. Fog and low cloud grounded Allied aircraft. The Germans broke through in several places; English-speaking German commandos in American uniforms spread confusion. On 17 December SS troops of Kampfgruppe Peiper shot over 80 American prisoners near Malmedy. American units at St. Vith and elsewhere fought delaying actions that disrupted the German timetable. Eisenhower rushed reinforcements to the area. Within days a salient, the "bulge", had been pushed some 80 kilometres into Allied lines.

episode: The Siege of Bastogne Begins
headline: Bastogne is surrounded
article: On 20 December German forces surrounded the town of Bastogne, a crossroads in the Belgian Ardennes, held by the 101st Airborne Division and elements of armoured divisions. On 22 December the Germans demanded surrender; the American commander, General Anthony McAuliffe, replied: "Nuts!" At a conference in Verdun on 19 December, Patton promised to turn his Third Army north and attack the southern flank of the Bulge within days, and did. On 23 December the weather cleared, allowing Allied aircraft to attack German columns and supply Bastogne by air. The German spearheads were running out of fuel near the Meuse. The siege made the 101st Airborne famous.

episode: Budapest Under Siege
headline: Budapest besieged; Bastogne relieved
article: On 26 December Patton's 4th Armored Division broke through to Bastogne from the south. The same day, Soviet forces completed the encirclement of Budapest, trapping around 70,000 German and Hungarian troops and 800,000 civilians. Hitler refused to let the city's defenders break out. The siege would last seven weeks and be one of the bloodiest city battles of the war. In the Ardennes, the German 2nd Panzer Division, closest to the Meuse, was destroyed near Celles by American and British armour. The German offensive had failed; the question now was how fast the Allies could reduce the Bulge. Germany's last reserves in the west had been spent.

episode: 1945 Begins!
headline: 1945 begins
article: On 1 January the Luftwaffe launched Operation Bodenplatte, a mass attack on Allied airfields in Belgium and the Netherlands. It destroyed many aircraft on the ground but lost around 300 German planes and many irreplaceable pilots. The same night, the Germans began Operation Nordwind against the US Seventh Army in Alsace, which had been weakened to help in the Ardennes. Eisenhower considered giving up Strasbourg; de Gaulle insisted it be held. In the Ardennes, the Allies began attacking the Bulge from the north and south. In the Philippines, MacArthur's forces prepared to land on Luzon. Germany still had the capacity to strike, but no longer to win.

episode: Soviet and American Massive Attacks
headline: The Vistula–Oder offensive
article: On 12 January the First Ukrainian Front under Konev attacked from its Vistula bridgehead at Sandomierz, and on 14 January the First Belorussian Front under Zhukov attacked from bridgeheads south of Warsaw. The German front collapsed in days. Soviet tank armies advanced up to 70 kilometres a day across Poland in winter weather. The offensive had been brought forward, Stalin later claimed, to help the Western Allies in the Ardennes. On 9 January American troops landed in the Lingayen Gulf on Luzon. In the Ardennes, the US First and Third Armies met at Houffalize on 16 January, cutting the Bulge in half.

episode: The Red Army Overruns Poland!
headline: The Red Army overruns Poland
article: On 17 January Soviet and Polish troops entered the ruins of Warsaw, which had been almost totally destroyed. Kraków, whose historic centre the Germans had abandoned largely intact, fell on 19 January, and Łódź the same day. In the east, the East Prussian offensive had begun on 13 January, and millions of Germans began fleeing west in freezing weather. Many fled too late, because Nazi officials had forbidden evacuation, and were caught by Soviet troops, who committed mass rapes and killings. In the Ardennes, the Bulge had been eliminated by late January; the Americans had suffered about 80,000 casualties. Whole provinces of eastern Germany were emptying.

episode: Himmler Takes Command
headline: Auschwitz is liberated
article: On 27 January soldiers of the Soviet 60th Army reached Auschwitz, the largest of the German camps, near the Polish town of Oświęcim. They found about 7,000 prisoners, most of them sick and starving, left behind when the SS had forced some 58,000 others on death marches west in the preceding days. Around 1.1 million people had been murdered there, about one million of them Jews, as well as Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and others. The SS had blown up the gas chambers and burned records, but warehouses still held hundreds of thousands of garments and huge quantities of human hair. 27 January is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day. This entry is shown without map styling.

episode: Is the Red Army Too Fast For its Own Good?
headline: Is the Red Army too fast?
article: By the end of January Zhukov's spearheads had reached the Oder river at Küstrin, about 70 kilometres from Berlin, and seized small bridgeheads on the far bank. Some Soviet commanders wanted to drive on to Berlin at once. But Soviet supply lines were stretched, the spring thaw was coming, and strong German forces in Pomerania threatened Zhukov's northern flank. Stalin halted the drive. On 30 January the liner Wilhelm Gustloff, carrying around 10,000 refugees and military personnel from East Prussia, was torpedoed by a Soviet submarine in the Baltic; over 9,000 died, the largest loss of life in a single ship sinking in history.

episode: The Battle of Manila Begins
headline: Yalta; the battle for Manila
article: From 4 to 11 February Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met at Yalta in Crimea. They agreed on the occupation of Germany in zones, with France getting one; on the founding conference of the United Nations; and that the USSR would join the war against Japan within three months of Germany's defeat, in return for territory in the Far East. On Poland, Stalin agreed to "free and unfettered elections", which never came. In Manila, American forces entered the city on 3 February; the battle for Manila lasted a month. Japanese naval troops who refused to withdraw killed some 100,000 Filipino civilians.

episode: German Counterattack in Pomerania
headline: Dresden is bombed
article: On the night of 13–14 February RAF Bomber Command attacked Dresden in two waves, and the US Eighth Air Force followed with daylight raids on 14 and 15 February. The attacks created a firestorm that destroyed much of the historic city centre. Around 25,000 people were killed, according to a historians' commission in 2010; Nazi propaganda claimed far higher numbers, and inflated figures persisted for decades. Dresden was a rail and communications centre for the Eastern Front, but the scale of destruction so late in the war became one of the most debated actions of the Allied bombing campaign. Churchill himself questioned it in a memo in March. In Pomerania, a German counterattack, Operation Solstice, briefly struck at Zhukov's flank.

episode: Iwo Jima!
headline: Iwo Jima
article: On 19 February US Marines landed on Iwo Jima, a small volcanic island halfway between the Marianas and Japan, wanted as an emergency airfield for B-29s and a base for escort fighters. The Japanese garrison of about 21,000 under General Tadamichi Kuribayashi had dug miles of tunnels and bunkers and did not contest the beaches, waiting until they were crowded with men and equipment. On 23 February Marines raised the US flag on Mount Suribachi, captured in a photograph by Joe Rosenthal that became famous worldwide. The fighting lasted five weeks. Almost all of the Japanese garrison died; about 6,800 Americans were killed.

episode: Allied Deception Surrounds Japanese in Burma
headline: Slim's deception in Burma
article: In Burma, General Slim's Fourteenth Army crossed the Irrawaddy river in February. Slim had concealed the true direction of his main attack: while the Japanese expected the main blow toward Mandalay, his IV Corps moved secretly south and struck at Meiktila, a key supply and communications centre. It fell on 3 March after fierce fighting. The Japanese 15th Army was cut off from its supply base, and the Japanese counterattacked desperately for weeks. In Europe, the US Ninth Army crossed the Roer river on 23 February as the floodwaters from the dams receded, and the Allies closed in on the Rhine.

episode: German Blunder Hands Allies a Rhine Crossing
headline: The bridge at Remagen
article: On 7 March a platoon of the US 9th Armored Division reached the Rhine at Remagen and found the Ludendorff railway bridge still standing. German engineers' demolition charges failed to bring it down, and American troops rushed across and established a bridgehead on the eastern bank. Eisenhower said it was "worth its weight in gold". Hitler had several officers executed for failing to destroy it. The bridge itself collapsed on 17 March, killing 28 American engineers, but by then pontoon bridges were in place. The same week Cologne fell to the US First Army. In Hungary, the Germans prepared their last offensive of the war.

episode: Smiling Albert Takes Command
headline: Kesselring takes over in the west
article: On 10 March Hitler replaced Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt as commander in the west with Albert Kesselring, known as "Smiling Albert", who had commanded in Italy. Kesselring told his officers he was the new V-3, a joke about the vengeance weapons. In Hungary, on 6 March, the Germans launched Operation Spring Awakening near Lake Balaton to protect the last oil fields still available to them; it stalled within days in mud and against Soviet defences. In the Pacific, on the night of 9–10 March, US B-29s dropped incendiaries on Tokyo, killing around 100,000 people in the deadliest single air raid in history.

episode: Chiang Versus Mountbatten
headline: Chiang versus Mountbatten
article: In Burma, British and Indian troops took Mandalay on 20 March after fighting for Fort Dufferin. Disagreements between Allied leaders over Burma intensified: Chiang Kai-shek wanted Chinese and American forces in northern Burma withdrawn to China to face the Japanese there, while Admiral Louis Mountbatten, the Allied commander in South-East Asia, wanted to push on to Rangoon before the monsoon. American transport aircraft, essential to Slim's supply, were also wanted in China. In Germany, the Western Allies cleared the west bank of the Rhine, and Patton's troops crossed the Rhine at Oppenheim on the night of 22 March. The race was now against the weather as well as the Japanese.

episode: Allies Charge Forward from the Rhine!
headline: Crossing the Rhine
article: On the night of 23–24 March Montgomery's 21st Army Group crossed the Rhine near Wesel in Operation Plunder, after a massive artillery bombardment. On the morning of 24 March two airborne divisions landed east of the river in Operation Varsity. Churchill watched from the west bank and crossed in a boat. Further south, American bridgeheads at Remagen and Oppenheim expanded. German resistance on the Rhine was patchy, and Allied armour began to break out into the German interior. On 19 March Hitler issued the "Nero Decree" ordering the destruction of Germany's infrastructure; Albert Speer worked to undermine it. The last natural barrier in western Germany had fallen.

episode: The Battle of Okinawa Begins
headline: The Battle of Okinawa begins
article: On 1 April American forces landed on Okinawa, an island of the Ryukyus about 550 kilometres from Japan, to use as a base for the invasion of Japan. The landing was unopposed: the Japanese had pulled back into strong defensive lines in the south of the island. The fighting that followed lasted almost three months. Kamikaze attacks on the US fleet offshore were heavier than ever. On 7 April American aircraft sank the battleship Yamato, sent on a one-way mission to Okinawa with fuel for a single voyage. Around 100,000 Okinawan civilians died in the battle, some forced to kill themselves by Japanese troops.

episode: Soviets Take Vienna and Königsberg
headline: Vienna and Königsberg fall; Roosevelt dies
article: On 9 April the German garrison of Königsberg, the capital of East Prussia, surrendered after a four-day assault. On 13 April Soviet forces took Vienna after a week of street fighting. On 12 April President Franklin D. Roosevelt died of a cerebral haemorrhage at Warm Springs, Georgia, and Harry Truman, his vice-president for less than three months, became president. Goebbels told Hitler it was the turning point foretold in the stars. On 11 April American troops liberated the concentration camp at Buchenwald, and on 15 April British troops entered Bergen-Belsen, where they found tens of thousands of sick and dying prisoners.

episode: Soviet Berlin Offensive Begins
headline: The Soviet assault on Berlin begins
article: Early on 16 April Zhukov's First Belorussian Front opened the Berlin offensive with one of the heaviest artillery bombardments in history from its Oder bridgehead at Küstrin. Searchlights were turned on the German positions to blind the defenders; instead they lit up the Soviet troops in the smoke. The German defenders on the Seelow Heights, having pulled back before the bombardment, held for three days, inflicting heavy losses. To the south, Konev's First Ukrainian Front crossed the Neisse river and made faster progress, and Stalin let him turn north toward Berlin, setting off a race between the two marshals. It was the last great battle of the war in Europe.

episode: 300,000 Germans Surrender in the Ruhr
headline: The Ruhr pocket surrenders
article: On 1 April the US First and Ninth Armies had met at Lippstadt, encircling Field Marshal Walter Model's Army Group B in the Ruhr industrial region. The pocket was compressed through mid-April, and on 18 April resistance ended. Over 300,000 German soldiers were taken prisoner. Model dissolved his army group and on 21 April shot himself in a forest near Duisburg. American forces reached the Elbe at Magdeburg on 11 April, but Eisenhower had decided to leave Berlin to the Soviets. British troops reached the outskirts of Bremen and Hamburg. In Italy, the final Allied offensive had broken through the German lines.

episode: The Battle of Berlin!
headline: The Battle of Berlin; Elbe Day at Torgau
article: On 20 April, Hitler's 56th birthday, Soviet artillery began to shell Berlin. By 25 April Soviet forces had encircled the city. Inside, the defence relied on remnants of army units, SS, Volkssturm and Hitler Youth. On 25 April American and Soviet troops met on the Elbe at Torgau and Strehla, cutting Germany in two; the meeting was celebrated with handshakes, toasts and photographs. In Italy, partisans rose in Milan, Turin and Genoa. On 28 April Mussolini, caught by partisans while trying to escape to Switzerland, was shot with his mistress Clara Petacci; their bodies were displayed hanging in a Milan square.

episode: The Death of Adolf Hitler
bigboard: Elbe Day at Torgau; Mussolini killed; Italy collapses; The fall of Berlin
headline: Hitler is dead; Berlin falls
photo: f:Raising a flag over the Reichstag - Restoration.jpg
article: On 30 April, with Soviet troops a few hundred metres away, Hitler shot himself in his bunker under the Reich Chancellery; his wife, Eva Braun, whom he had married the day before, took poison. Their bodies were burned in the garden. That evening Soviet soldiers raised a flag over the Reichstag; the famous photograph was restaged on 2 May. Berlin's garrison surrendered on 2 May, the same day German forces in Italy surrendered. Admiral Dönitz, named Hitler's successor, tried to delay surrender so that as many Germans as possible could reach the Western Allies. Germany surrendered unconditionally at Reims on 7 May and in Berlin on 8 May. The war in Europe was over.
